  4. (D)Declining cities should concentrate services in occupied districts and turn empty blocks into parks, since trying to attract new industry is always a waste of public money.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph compares two responses to population loss, gives each a cost ('Neither is costless'), and then judges that 'only the second is honest about the likely future of many such places'. The correct answer keeps the preference, the admitted costs and the scope ('many').

Why not (B): The paragraph mentions that the second approach 'risks being read as surrender' as a cost, not as its conclusion, and it ends by favouring that approach, so this reverses it.

Why not (C): This reports the comparison but drops the verdict in the last sentence that 'only the second is honest about the likely future of many such places'.

Why not (D): The paragraph says growth schemes 'often' spend on growth that never arrives, not always, and it admits the second approach has costs; 'always a waste' overstates it.

Common misconception: Choosing the even-handed comparison and missing that the paragraph ends with a verdict.

Difficulty: A neutral wrong option describes the comparison accurately; it is wrong only because the paragraph takes a side in its final clause. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-059 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A familiar principle in ethics holds that 'ought' implies 'can': it makes no sense to say that someone ought to do what they are unable to do. Nobody blames a person for failing to rescue a drowning child from a river on the other side of the world. The principle seems obvious, but it needs care. A man who could have repaid a loan but carelessly made himself unable to, by spending the money he had set aside for it, is not excused by his present inability. What the principle rules out, properly understood, is an obligation that was never within a person's power to meet, not an obligation that a person has put beyond his own reach.

  1. (A)The principle that duty requires ability is mistaken, since people are often rightly blamed for failing to do things that they were in fact unable to do.
  2. (B)Inability cancels a duty only when the person never had the power to meet it, not when the person has carelessly made the duty impossible.
  3. (C)Nobody can reasonably be blamed for failing to rescue a drowning child whom they could not possibly have reached in time to save from the water.
  4. (D)Whenever people are unable to do what is asked of them, they cannot be blamed for failing, whatever the reason they now find themselves unable to act.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph states the principle, grants its obvious core, and then refines it with the example of the man who spent the money for his loan: what the principle rules out is an obligation 'never within a person's power to meet, not an obligation that a person has put beyond his own reach'. The correct answer states exactly this refinement.

Why not (A): The paragraph keeps the principle and says it 'needs care'; it narrows what the principle rules out rather than calling it mistaken.

Why not (C): This restates the opening illustration only; it misses the refinement that makes up the rest of the paragraph, so it is too narrow.

Why not (D): The paragraph denies that inability always excuses: the man who spent the money set aside for his loan 'is not excused by his present inability'.

Common misconception: Choosing the unqualified version of the principle, which the paragraph sets up only to refine.

Difficulty: The refinement is stated outright in the last sentence; wrong options are the unrefined principle, the opening example and a reversal. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-060 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is widely held that a hypocrite has no standing to blame: the smoker who lectures his son about cigarettes, we say, should keep quiet. There is something right in this. Blame from someone who excuses the same fault in himself rings false, and it invites the reply 'Look who is talking'. But the view goes wrong if it implies that the criticism itself is mistaken. The son's smoking is no healthier because his father smokes, and a fault does not become acceptable merely because the person naming it shares it. What hypocrisy damages is the critic's authority to demand change, not the truth of what he says, and even that damage can be repaired if the critic admits his own failing. A hypocrite who says 'I do it too, and I am wrong to' has not forfeited the right to speak.

  1. (A)A hypocrite's criticism may be correct but carries no weight, and since nothing can restore his authority, he should leave the task of blaming to others.
  2. (B)People who share a fault have no right to criticise it in others, because blame from anyone guilty of the same failing always rings false to those who hear it.
  3. (C)Since a criticism is no less true when the critic shares the fault, hypocrisy does nothing to weaken anyone's standing to blame other people for that fault.
  4. (D)Hypocrisy weakens a critic's authority to demand change but not the correctness of the criticism, and a critic who admits sharing the fault can recover the standing to speak.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph separates two things the common view runs together: the truth of a criticism, which hypocrisy leaves untouched ('The son's smoking is no healthier because his father smokes'), and the critic's 'authority to demand change', which hypocrisy damages. It then adds that this damage 'can be repaired' by admitting the fault. The correct answer holds all three parts; each wrong option gets one part wrong.

Why not (A): The paragraph says the damage to authority 'can be repaired if the critic admits his own failing', so the claim that nothing can restore it is false.

Why not (B): This is the widely held view the paragraph qualifies; it ends by saying a hypocrite who admits the fault 'has not forfeited the right to speak'.

Why not (C): The paragraph grants 'There is something right in this' and says hypocrisy 'damages' the critic's authority to demand change, so 'does nothing to weaken' contradicts it.

Common misconception: Choosing the option that defends the criticism's truth and overlooking that the paragraph does concede a real loss of authority.

Difficulty: Each wrong option is right about one of the paragraph's three claims and wrong about another; the reader must track the distinction between truth and authority and the closing repair. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-061 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Can the dead be harmed? The sceptic replies that harm requires someone to suffer it, and the dead suffer nothing. Yet we do seem to wrong a person when, after her death, we break the promise we made to her, scatter the collection she spent her life assembling, or spread lies about her. One way to make sense of this is to notice that many of our interests are not interests in experiences. A woman who wants her life's work to survive wants something to be true of the world, not merely to feel that it is; that is why being deceived about it during her lifetime would also harm her. If interests of this kind can be set back without the person's knowledge, then death, which ends experience, need not end every interest.

  1. (A)The dead can be harmed because some form of experience continues after death, which is why lies told about them seem to wrong them so deeply.
  2. (B)A person who wants her life's work to survive is harmed if she is deceived about its fate, even if she never discovers the deception during her life.
  3. (C)Because many interests concern how the world goes rather than what a person experiences, they can be set back after death, so the dead may genuinely be harmed.
  4. (D)Since harm needs someone who suffers it and the dead experience nothing, breaking promises made to them can wrong only the living people who remember them.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph answers the sceptic by noting that 'many of our interests are not interests in experiences'; such interests can be set back 'without the person's knowledge', as the case of deception shows, so 'death, which ends experience, need not end every interest'. The correct answer gives the premise and the conclusion together.

Why not (A): The paragraph describes death as that 'which ends experience' and rests its case on interests that do not depend on experience, so this contradicts its reasoning.

Why not (B): This is the supporting case about deception during a lifetime; it omits the conclusion about death, so it is too narrow.

Why not (D): This is the sceptic's reply from the second sentence, extended; the paragraph argues against it by distinguishing interests from experiences.

Common misconception: Choosing the deception example because it is the paragraph's most concrete step, and missing the conclusion it leads to.

Difficulty: The argument is abstract and runs through an analogy; one wrong option is the analogy without the conclusion. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-062 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Pity and compassion are often treated as the same feeling, but they place the one who feels them differently. Pity looks down. It registers another's misfortune from a position of safety, and it often carries a quiet relief that the misfortune belongs to someone else; this is why people who are pitied so often resent it. Compassion stands alongside. It begins from the recognition that the other person's suffering is the kind of thing that could befall anyone, oneself included, and so it treats the sufferer as an equal rather than as an object of concern. The difference is not that one is warmer than the other, for pity can be intensely felt. It is that only compassion leaves the dignity of the sufferer intact.

  1. (A)Pity is a selfish emotion that ought to be suppressed entirely, since it involves relief at another's suffering and treats the sufferer as an object of concern.
  2. (B)People who are pitied often resent it, because pity registers their misfortune from a position of safety and carries relief that the misfortune is not one's own.
  3. (C)Compassion is a deeper and warmer feeling than pity, which is why people who are pitied resent it while those who receive compassion feel respected by it.
  4. (D)Pity and compassion differ less in intensity than in stance: pity regards the sufferer from above, while compassion sees an equal and so preserves the sufferer's dignity.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph contrasts the two feelings by where they place the one who feels them: pity 'looks down', compassion 'stands alongside'. It then rules out the obvious alternative ('not that one is warmer than the other') and ends with the real difference: 'only compassion leaves the dignity of the sufferer intact'. The correct answer captures the stance contrast and the denial that it is about warmth.

Why not (A): The paragraph says pity 'often' carries relief, not always, and it recommends nothing; calling it selfish and urging its suppression goes beyond the text.

Why not (B): This describes pity alone and leaves out compassion and the contrast that is the paragraph's point, so it is too narrow.

Why not (C): The paragraph says 'The difference is not that one is warmer than the other, for pity can be intensely felt', so this misstates the basis of the contrast.

Common misconception: Picking the option that ranks compassion as warmer, which the paragraph explicitly denies.

Difficulty: The tempting wrong option states the contrast in terms of warmth, which the paragraph rules out in one clause near the end. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-063 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Impostor feelings, the private conviction that one's success is undeserved and will soon be exposed, are commonly described as a disorder of self-perception to be corrected by building confidence. The description fits some cases. But it treats as a fault in the individual a response that is often a reasonable reading of the situation. A first-generation student surrounded by peers who seem to know unspoken rules, or the only woman in a department, may feel out of place because she has been placed in a setting that signals, in many small ways, that she does not belong. Confidence training alone asks her to stop noticing those signals. It would be wiser to treat persistent impostor feelings as information about environments as well as about the people in them.

  1. (A)First-generation students and women in departments dominated by men are especially likely to feel that their success is undeserved and will soon be exposed.
  2. (B)Impostor feelings are not only a distorted self-image but often a sensible response to settings signalling exclusion, so they also carry information about environments.
  3. (C)Impostor feelings are a distorted way of seeing oneself, and the best remedy is training that builds the confidence of the individuals who privately experience them.
  4. (D)Impostor feelings are never really about the individual but are created entirely by unwelcoming institutions, so confidence training is pointless and should be abandoned.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph reports the usual view (a disorder of self-perception, fixed by confidence), grants that it 'fits some cases', and then argues that the feelings are 'often a reasonable reading of the situation' in settings that signal non-belonging. It concludes that they should be treated as 'information about environments as well as about the people in them'. The correct answer keeps the reinterpretation, its hedges and the conclusion.

Why not (A): These are illustrations, and the paragraph makes no claim about which groups are most likely to have such feelings; the option misses its point about remedies.

Why not (C): This is the common description the paragraph says fits only 'some cases'; it argues that confidence training 'alone' misses what the feelings reveal about environments.

Why not (D): The paragraph concedes that the individual description 'fits some cases' and asks for attention to environments 'as well as' people, so 'never' and 'entirely' overstate it.

Common misconception: Swinging from the individual view to the opposite extreme and ignoring 'fits some cases' and 'as well as'.

Difficulty: The correct answer and the extreme wrong option share the reinterpretation; they differ only in degree, which turns on two short qualifiers. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-064 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

People asked about a recent decision usually regret what they did more than what they failed to do: the hasty purchase or the unwise remark stings more than the opportunity let pass. Asked to look back over their lives, however, many report the reverse; the courses not taken, the things left unsaid, come to dominate. One explanation is that the consequences of an action are bounded and visible, so they can be repaired, excused or absorbed into a story of learning, while the consequences of inaction remain open, an unlived alternative that imagination keeps improving. If so, the familiar finding that actions are regretted more is not false, but it describes only the short run; over time the balance appears to shift.

  1. (A)Actions tend to be regretted more in the short term but inactions more over a lifetime, perhaps because unchosen paths stay open to imagination while the results of actions are settled.
  2. (B)Because the results of actions can be repaired or excused, people regret their actions less as time passes and, in the end, cease to regret them at all.
  3. (C)People regret what they fail to do more than what they actually do, so the familiar claim that actions are regretted more reflects a mistake about human memory.
  4. (D)Short-term regret centres on actions and long-term regret on inactions, which shows that memory distorts the past and makes early judgements of our choices unreliable.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph reports a finding (recent decisions: actions regretted more), sets beside it a reversal over a lifetime ('many report the reverse'), offers a tentative explanation ('One explanation is', 'If so'), and concludes that the familiar finding 'describes only the short run'. The correct answer keeps both time scales, the tentative cause and the hedged tone; the closest wrong option has the right pattern but attaches an explanation the paragraph does not give.

Why not (B): The paragraph says only that 'the balance appears to shift' towards inaction; it never says regret for actions disappears, and the option drops inaction entirely.

Why not (C): The paragraph says the familiar finding 'is not false' but 'describes only the short run', so declaring it a mistake reverses the paragraph's qualification.

Why not (D): The first half is right, but the paragraph explains the shift by the open-endedness of inaction, not by a failure of memory, and it says the short-run finding 'is not false', so it does not call early judgements unreliable.

Common misconception: Accepting the first half of an option and not checking the explanation it adds.

Difficulty: Two wrong options have the correct short-run and long-run pattern in part; one is separated from the correct answer only by the cause it supplies. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-065 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

People rarely judge their own situation in isolation; they compare it with that of others, and the others they choose are usually those slightly better off. Such upward comparison can motivate, since a colleague who is a little more skilled shows what is within reach. But when the comparison is constant and the gap seems fixed, it breeds dissatisfaction even among people who are doing well by any absolute measure. A worker whose salary rises may feel poorer if her neighbours' salaries rise faster. Contentment, on this account, depends less on what one has than on whom one measures oneself against.

  1. (A)A worker whose pay increases may still feel poorer than before if the neighbours living around her are receiving larger increases each year than her own.
  2. (B)People usually compare themselves with those who are worse off, which motivates them to work harder and keeps them content even when their own incomes fall.
  3. (C)Since people measure themselves against those slightly better off, contentment depends on whom they compare with; such comparison can motivate but, when constant, breeds discontent.
  4. (D)Comparing oneself with others is always harmful, since it makes even prosperous people dissatisfied, so people should judge their lives by absolute standards of wealth alone.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph explains a phenomenon: people compare 'upward', which 'can motivate' but, when constant, 'breeds dissatisfaction even among people who are doing well'. Its conclusion is that contentment 'depends less on what one has than on whom one measures oneself against'. The correct answer keeps the mechanism, both effects and the conclusion.

Why not (A): This is the illustration in the fourth sentence; it omits the general claim about comparison and its two effects, so it is too narrow.

Why not (B): The paragraph says people compare with 'those slightly better off', so this reverses the direction of comparison and its effect.

Why not (D): The paragraph says upward comparison 'can motivate', so 'always harmful' contradicts it, and it offers no advice about absolute standards.

Common misconception: Choosing the salary example, which is vivid but only illustrates the point.

Difficulty: The point is stated in the first and last sentences; each wrong option is a detail, an absolute or a reversal. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-066 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

For decades the belief that basketball players get a 'hot hand', becoming more likely to score after a run of successes, was a textbook example of people seeing patterns in randomness. Analyses of shooting records found that hits did not cluster more than chance would predict, and the belief was filed alongside other errors of intuition. Later work identified a subtle flaw in the way those records had been analysed: the method used was biased toward finding no streakiness. Corrected analyses suggest that a modest hot hand may exist after all. This does not vindicate the fans entirely, since the effect appears far smaller than players and spectators believe. The episode shows instead that a debunking can itself rest on an error, and that a belief may be exaggerated without being baseless.

  1. (A)People readily see patterns in random events, as belief in the basketball hot hand shows, since shooting records reveal no clustering of successful shots at all.
  2. (B)The hot hand, dismissed as an illusion, may exist in modest form once a flaw in earlier analyses is corrected, so the belief is exaggerated, not baseless.
  3. (C)Later research has shown that sports fans were right all along about the hot hand, and that the earlier studies dismissing it should now simply be disregarded.
  4. (D)Since debunkings can rest on errors, beliefs that experts dismiss as illusions usually turn out to be correct once the original evidence is analysed again.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph traces a finding and its revision: the hot hand was dismissed, a flaw in the method was found, and corrected analyses suggest 'a modest hot hand may exist after all'. It then qualifies the revision ('does not vindicate the fans entirely') and ends that the belief 'may be exaggerated without being baseless'. The correct answer keeps the revision and the qualification.

Why not (A): This is the earlier view the paragraph reports and then revises: corrected analyses 'suggest that a modest hot hand may exist after all'.

Why not (C): The paragraph says the correction 'does not vindicate the fans entirely', since the effect 'appears far smaller' than they believe, so 'right all along' overstates it.

Why not (D): The paragraph draws a lesson from one episode, that a debunking 'can' rest on an error; 'usually turn out to be correct' generalises far beyond it.

Common misconception: Treating the revision as a full vindication, or stopping at the earlier debunking reported in the first two sentences.

Difficulty: The paragraph moves through three positions; wrong options capture the first, an overstated second and an overgeneralised lesson. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-067 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

To a visitor used to fixed prices, haggling in a bazaar can look like inefficiency, a waste of time over sums too small to matter. For the trader it does useful work. In a market without price tags, the opening figure lets the seller learn what a customer is willing to pay, so that the wealthy visitor and the local regular can be charged differently without either being told so. The exchange also builds a relationship: a buyer who returns and bargains well is recognised, and the next deal starts from a friendlier figure. What seems like friction is, in such markets, the means by which prices are discovered and loyalty is formed.

  1. (A)Bazaar traders use haggling mainly to cheat wealthy visitors, charging them far more than local customers while pretending that the price is the same for all.
  2. (B)Haggling over small sums wastes the time of buyers and sellers alike, which is why most modern markets have replaced it with fixed and clearly labelled prices.
  3. (C)A buyer who returns to the same trader and bargains well is recognised, so that the next deal between them begins from a friendlier opening price.
  4. (D)Haggling, which outsiders see as wasteful, lets traders learn what each buyer will pay and build ties with returning customers, so it serves real purposes.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph contrasts the visitor's view of haggling as 'inefficiency' with the work it does for the trader: it discovers what each customer will pay and builds a relationship with returning buyers. The last sentence sums up: what 'seems like friction' is how 'prices are discovered and loyalty is formed'. The correct answer states both functions against the outsider's view.

Why not (A): The paragraph notes that different buyers can be charged differently but treats this as price discovery, not cheating; the moral charge and 'mainly' are added.

Why not (B): This is the visitor's impression that the paragraph sets aside; the claim about modern markets replacing haggling is not made at all.

Why not (C): This is one of the two functions the paragraph describes; it leaves out price discovery and the general point, so it is too narrow.

Common misconception: Choosing the relationship detail, which is only half of what the paragraph claims.

Difficulty: The two functions are named in the final sentence; wrong options are the rejected view, a moral distortion and one half. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-068 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It has become common advice that anyone with a hobby should turn it into a side income: sell the pottery, charge for the baking, open a channel for the guitar playing. The advice is not foolish, and for some people a pastime becomes a satisfying second livelihood. But it rests on the assumption that an activity is improved by acquiring a market price, and for many people the opposite is true. A hobby is valuable partly because nothing depends on it; one can do it badly, stop for a month, or follow a whim without disappointing anyone. Once customers, ratings and deadlines arrive, the activity begins to resemble the work it once offered relief from. Some pursuits are worth keeping precisely because they earn nothing.

  1. (A)Turning hobbies into income suits some people, but for many it destroys what made the hobby valuable, its freedom from obligation, by making it resemble ordinary work.
  2. (B)Hobbies are valuable mainly because people can do them badly or drop them for a month, which is why they make poor businesses that seldom earn money.
  3. (C)People should never sell what they make in their spare time, since earning money from any activity inevitably destroys the pleasure it once gave them.
  4. (D)A hobby is a valuable source of extra income, and people who develop their pastimes into small businesses often find in them a satisfying second livelihood.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph reports common advice, concedes that it works for 'some people', and then challenges its assumption: a hobby is valuable 'partly because nothing depends on it', and once customers and deadlines arrive it 'begins to resemble the work it once offered relief from'. The correct answer keeps the concession, the scope 'many' and the reason.

Why not (B): The paragraph says a hobby is valuable 'partly', not mainly, because nothing depends on it, and it says nothing about hobbies making poor businesses or earning little; that conclusion is added.

Why not (C): The paragraph grants that 'for some people a pastime becomes a satisfying second livelihood', so 'never' and 'inevitably' contradict it.

Why not (D): This is the common advice and its best case, which the paragraph concedes for 'some people' before arguing that for many 'the opposite is true'.

Common misconception: Taking the conceded best case, stated early, for the paragraph's view.

Difficulty: A concession and a reported view precede the argument; one wrong option borrows the argument's premise and attaches an outside conclusion. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-069 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When offices relax their dress codes, the change is usually welcomed as a move towards equality: without suits and ties, the argument goes, the junior clerk and the senior partner look alike, and people are judged by their work rather than their clothes. The intention is sincere, but the result is often a code that has become harder, not easier, to read. A formal rule could be learned once and followed by anyone who could afford a suit; the new norms, which separate the right kind of casual from the wrong kind, are rarely written down and are absorbed mostly by those already at home in the social world that sets them. The newcomer who arrives in the wrong trainers has broken no stated rule and cannot easily find out which unstated one she has broken. Relaxing a code, in short, need not relax its power to sort people; it may only make that power less visible.

  1. (A)Abolishing suits and ties in offices removes the visible markers of rank, so that junior and senior staff look alike and are judged mainly on the quality of their work.
  2. (B)Relaxed dress codes, though meant to equalise, often swap learnable written rules for unwritten ones that favour insiders, so clothing may sort people as before, only less visibly.
  3. (C)Casual dress codes are adopted insincerely by employers who wish to keep newcomers out of senior roles while appearing to treat all their staff as equals.
  4. (D)Offices should return to formal dress codes, because written rules about clothing are fairer than casual norms and can be followed by anyone who wishes to.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph reports the egalitarian case for relaxed codes, grants that 'The intention is sincere', and argues that the result is often harder to read: formal rules could be 'learned once', while casual norms are unwritten and 'absorbed mostly by those already at home' in the world that sets them. Its conclusion is hedged: relaxing a code 'need not relax its power to sort people; it may only make that power less visible'. The correct answer keeps the sincere intention, the mechanism, the hedges and the conclusion.

Why not (A): This is the hope the paragraph reports in its first sentence; it goes on to argue that the result is 'often a code that has become harder, not easier, to read'.

Why not (C): The paragraph says 'The intention is sincere'; the sorting it describes is an unintended effect of unwritten norms, not a hidden aim.

Why not (D): The paragraph prescribes nothing, and it limits the virtue of formal rules to those 'who could afford a suit', so 'anyone who wishes to' and the recommendation both go beyond it.

Common misconception: Choosing the prescription to restore formal codes, which reads the comparison as a recommendation, or the insincerity reading, which ignores an explicit concession.

Difficulty: Two wrong options are close inferences a reader might draw (go back to formal codes; the policy is a cover) and are ruled out only by a short concession and the limited claim made for formal rules. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-070 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Small towns are often praised for their closeness: everyone knows your name, and help is never far away. Large cities are faulted for the opposite, a crowd in which no one notices whether you thrive or fail. The contrast is fair as far as it goes, but it leaves out what anonymity gives. To be known by everyone is also to be watched by everyone, and for a young person whose ambitions, beliefs or way of life depart from the local norm, the town's closeness can feel like a cage. The indifference of the city is what allows such people to try out a new self without asking permission. Loneliness is a real cost of urban life, but it is the price of a freedom that intimate communities rarely offer.

  1. (A)Urban anonymity, usually counted only as a cause of loneliness, also gives people who depart from local norms a freedom that close-knit towns seldom allow.
  2. (B)Anonymity makes city life better than small town life in every respect, since the loneliness that people complain of in large cities is largely imagined.
  3. (C)Young people whose ambitions or beliefs differ from those of their home town often experience its closeness as a cage from which they long to escape.
  4. (D)Large cities are lonely places where nobody notices anyone else, whereas small towns provide the closeness and ready help that people need in order to thrive.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph accepts the usual contrast as 'fair as far as it goes', then adds what it omits: being known is also being watched, and the city's indifference lets nonconforming people 'try out a new self'. It ends by weighing the two: loneliness is 'a real cost' but 'the price of a freedom that intimate communities rarely offer'. The correct answer keeps the added point and the concession.

Why not (B): The paragraph calls loneliness 'a real cost of urban life', so calling it imagined, and the city better 'in every respect', contradicts it.

Why not (C): This is one step of the argument; it leaves out the city's side of the comparison and the weighing of loneliness against freedom, so it is too narrow.

Why not (D): This is the familiar contrast the paragraph calls 'fair as far as it goes' before adding what it 'leaves out', the freedom anonymity gives.

Common misconception: Choosing the extreme option because it favours the city, which seems to be the paragraph's side, without noticing it denies the conceded cost.

Difficulty: The paragraph takes a side while conceding a cost; the extreme wrong option is on the right side but drops the concession. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-071 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Historians divide the past into periods, and the names they choose do more than organise it. To call a thousand years of European history the 'Middle Ages' is to describe them as an interval between two more important times, a long pause between the classical world and its supposed rebirth. The label was coined by people who wished to see themselves as reviving antiquity, and it carried their judgement into textbooks for centuries. Periods are indispensable; without them the past would be an undifferentiated stream. But a period name is never a neutral container. It embeds a view about what mattered, and the historian who uses it without noticing this inherits a verdict rather than reaching one.

  1. (A)Historians should abandon period labels such as the 'Middle Ages', since dividing the past into named periods inevitably distorts how students and scholars understand it.
  2. (B)Because history without periods would be an undifferentiated stream, the names that historians give to periods are neutral containers that help to organise the past.
  3. (C)The term 'Middle Ages' was coined by people who saw themselves as reviving antiquity, and it presents a thousand years as a pause between two greater eras.
  4. (D)Period labels are needed to organise history, yet they carry their coiners' judgements, so historians who use them unthinkingly adopt verdicts they never examined.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph uses the 'Middle Ages' to show that period names 'do more than organise' the past. It concedes that 'Periods are indispensable', but insists that a name 'embeds a view about what mattered', so a historian who uses it unawares 'inherits a verdict rather than reaching one'. The correct answer keeps the concession and the warning.

Why not (A): The paragraph says 'Periods are indispensable'; its complaint is against using names 'without noticing' what they embed, not against periods or names as such.

Why not (B): The paragraph says the reverse: 'a period name is never a neutral container', even though periods themselves are indispensable.

Why not (C): This is the example the paragraph uses; it leaves out the general claim about all period names and what historians inherit, so it is too narrow.

Common misconception: Choosing the option that rejects period labels altogether, which ignores the concession that periods are indispensable.

Difficulty: The concession and the warning sit in adjacent sentences; one wrong option keeps the warning and drops the concession, another keeps the concession and drops the warning. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-072 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It seems obvious that famines happen when there is not enough food. Yet several major famines have occurred in regions where the total supply of food was not much lower than in normal years, and some while food was being exported. What collapsed was not the harvest but the ability of particular groups to obtain food: labourers whose wages fell, artisans whose customers vanished, herders whose animals lost value as grain prices rose. A famine, on this view, is less a shortage of food than a failure of access to it, concentrated on those whose means of buying or growing it have broken down. This does not mean harvests are irrelevant, for a poor harvest is often what sets the collapse in motion; it means that counting the grain is not enough to predict who will starve.

  1. (A)Harvest failures play no real part in causing famines, which are produced entirely by falling wages and the loss of customers among the poorest groups of people.
  2. (B)Famines occur when the total supply of food in a region falls below what its people need, so the size of the harvest is the best guide to who will starve.
  3. (C)Famines often stem less from an overall lack of food than from the collapse of particular groups' ability to obtain it, though a poor harvest may set that collapse off.
  4. (D)During famines, labourers, artisans and herders suffer most because their wages, customers and animals lose their value just as the price of grain is rising.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph challenges the view that famines are simply shortages: several have occurred without a large fall in total supply, and what failed was 'the ability of particular groups to obtain food'. It then qualifies the thesis: harvests are not 'irrelevant', since a poor one 'is often what sets the collapse in motion'. The correct answer keeps the reinterpretation and the qualification.

Why not (A): The paragraph says 'This does not mean harvests are irrelevant', since a poor harvest 'is often what sets the collapse in motion', so 'no real part' and 'entirely' contradict it.

Why not (B): This is the 'obvious' view the paragraph challenges; it ends by saying 'counting the grain is not enough to predict who will starve'.

Why not (D): These are the examples of collapsed access in the third sentence; the option omits the general reinterpretation and the place of harvests, so it is too narrow.

Common misconception: Choosing the absolute version that dismisses harvests, which overlooks the final sentence.

Difficulty: The thesis is clear, but the correct answer must be told apart from an extreme version by the closing qualification. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-073 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Before factories, most work was organised by the task rather than by the hour. A farmer milked when the cows needed milking, and a weaver at home worked hard before a delivery and slackly after it. The factory changed this because its machines were expensive and had to be kept running, which required many workers to be present at the same moment. Clocks, bells and fines for lateness taught people to treat time as something owned by the employer and measured in units. The punctuality now regarded as a personal virtue was, in large part, a discipline that industrial work had to impose.

  1. (A)Before factories, workers were idle and unreliable, and only clocks, bells and fines for lateness finally taught them the value of working hard every day.
  2. (B)A farmer milked his cows when they needed milking, and a weaver at home laboured hard before a delivery and slackly after it had been made.
  3. (C)Punctuality is a natural personal virtue, and factories prospered because they could attract and keep workers who already possessed that virtue in abundance.
  4. (D)Clock-measured work replaced task-based rhythms because costly factory machines needed workers present together, so punctuality began largely as imposed discipline.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph contrasts task-based work with factory time, gives the cause (expensive machines needing many workers 'present at the same moment'), names the means (clocks, bells, fines), and concludes that punctuality was 'in large part' imposed. The correct answer gives the change, its cause and the hedged conclusion.

Why not (A): The paragraph describes task-based work, in which people worked hard when the task required; it never calls earlier workers idle, and its point is about punctuality, not effort.

Why not (B): This restates the examples of task-based work in the second sentence and leaves out the change and its cause, so it is too narrow.

Why not (C): The paragraph says punctuality was 'in large part, a discipline that industrial work had to impose', which is the reverse of a virtue workers already had.

Common misconception: Picking the examples of pre-industrial work, which are vivid but only set up the contrast.

Difficulty: The causal chain runs in order through short sentences; wrong options are a detail, a reversal and a moral distortion. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-074 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many customs presented as ancient turn out, on inspection, to be quite recent: a ceremony said to go back centuries may have been devised a few generations ago, often at a moment when a group felt its identity threatened. Debunkers enjoy pointing this out, as if exposing the recent origin of a tradition exposed it as a fraud. The inference is too quick. A tradition does not need to be old to do what traditions do, which is to bind people to one another and to a shared past, and a recent invention that people adopt wholeheartedly is no less real in its effects than one inherited unbroken. What the discovery should change is not our regard for the practice but our belief about its history; the claim to antiquity may be false while the attachment it supports is genuine.

  1. (A)Traditions are usually invented when a group's identity is threatened, which explains why such new customs are adopted more wholeheartedly by their members than inherited ones.
  2. (B)Traditions that claim ancient roots but were in fact devised recently are frauds, since their whole appeal depends on a false story about their origins in the distant past.
  3. (C)Showing that a supposedly ancient tradition is recent should correct beliefs about its history, but it does not make the tradition a sham, since the bonds it creates are real.
  4. (D)Because recent traditions bind people as effectively as ancient ones, the false claims of antiquity attached to them are harmless and need not be corrected.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph reports a finding (many 'ancient' customs are recent), rejects the debunkers' inference that recency means fraud ('The inference is too quick'), and draws a two-sided conclusion: the discovery should change 'not our regard for the practice but our belief about its history'. The correct answer keeps both halves; the hardest wrong option keeps the first half and drops the second.

Why not (A): The paragraph says such inventions 'often' come at such moments and that adopted inventions are 'no less real', not more wholehearted; the comparison is added.

Why not (B): This is the debunkers' inference, which the paragraph calls 'too quick': a recent tradition can bind people just as an inherited one does.

Why not (D): The paragraph says the discovery 'should change' our 'belief about its history', so it does want the false claim corrected; only our regard for the practice should stay.

Common misconception: Choosing the option that defends recent traditions so fully that it excuses the false history, missing that the paragraph still wants the belief corrected.

Difficulty: The correct answer's two halves are each mirrored in a wrong option that keeps one and inverts the other; the reader must hold the closing distinction exactly. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-075 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The phrase 'the Silk Road' suggests a single highway along which caravans carried silk from China to Rome. The reality was a shifting web of routes, by land and sea, along which most goods travelled only short distances before changing hands. Few merchants made the whole journey; a bale might pass through a dozen markets, each trader knowing only the next stage. Silk was one commodity among many, and ideas, technologies and diseases moved along the same paths. The single name is convenient, but it can make a loose and long-lived network sound like a planned route.

  1. (A)Few merchants ever travelled the whole distance between China and Rome, so a bale of goods might pass through a dozen markets before it reached its final buyer.
  2. (B)The name 'Silk Road' can suggest one planned highway, but trade actually moved in short relays along a shifting web of land and sea routes, carrying many goods.
  3. (C)Silk was a minor commodity on the routes between China and Rome, which carried chiefly ideas, technologies and diseases rather than goods meant for sale.
  4. (D)Historians should stop using the name 'Silk Road' altogether, since it is a myth with no connection to any trade that really took place along those routes.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph contrasts what the name 'suggests' (a single highway carrying silk) with what it calls 'The reality': a shifting web of routes, short-distance relays and many kinds of cargo. It ends that the 'convenient' name can make a network 'sound like a planned route'. The correct answer states the contrast and its elements.

Why not (A): This is a supporting detail from the third sentence; it omits the paragraph's point about the misleading name, so it is too narrow.

Why not (C): The paragraph says silk was 'one commodity among many' and that 'most goods travelled only short distances', so goods were central; this distorts it.

Why not (D): The paragraph calls the name 'convenient' and describes real trade along the routes; it neither calls the trade a myth nor asks for the name to be dropped.

Common misconception: Choosing the detail about merchants, which supports the point but is not the point.

Difficulty: The contrast between name and reality is announced in the first two sentences and restated at the end. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-076 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Critics of choosing public officials by lot usually object that it ignores competence: a random citizen, they say, is no more fit to govern than a random passenger is to fly an aircraft. The objection assumes that election reliably selects for the relevant competence, and that assumption deserves more scrutiny than it receives. Elections reward the ability to win elections, which overlaps with the ability to deliberate well on public questions but is not the same thing; they also filter heavily for wealth, connections and an appetite for publicity. Lot has its own weaknesses, and nobody sensible proposes drawing a finance minister from a hat. But for bodies whose task is to weigh evidence and represent a cross-section of opinion, such as panels reviewing a contested policy, the comparison that matters is not lot against an ideal of expertise but lot against the electoral filter as it actually operates.

  1. (A)The objection that lot ignores competence assumes elections select for it; for deliberative bodies, lot should be weighed against how elections really filter, not against ideal expertise.
  2. (B)Selection by lot is better than election for every public office, because elections favour wealth, connections and a taste for publicity over genuine ability.
  3. (C)Since a random citizen is as unfit to govern as a random passenger is to fly, lot should be confined to advisory panels that hold no real authority.
  4. (D)Elections reward the skill of winning votes instead of the skill of deliberating, which is why elected officials are usually less competent than citizens chosen at random.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph reports the critics' objection, then attacks its hidden assumption that elections select for competence, noting that they reward 'the ability to win elections' and filter for wealth and publicity. It concedes lot's weaknesses and restricts its case to deliberative bodies, concluding that the right comparison is 'lot against the electoral filter as it actually operates'. The correct answer keeps the critique, the scope and the conclusion.

Why not (B): The paragraph limits its case to deliberative bodies and says 'nobody sensible proposes drawing a finance minister from a hat', so 'every public office' contradicts its stated scope.

Why not (C): The passenger analogy is the critics' view, which the paragraph scrutinises rather than accepts, and it says nothing about denying such panels authority.

Why not (D): The paragraph says the two abilities overlap 'but' are 'not the same thing'; it never claims elected officials are less competent than random citizens, so this overstates the point.

Common misconception: Choosing the option that turns a qualified critique of the objection into a sweeping endorsement of lot.

Difficulty: Needs the author's scope limit (deliberative bodies only) to reject the sweeping option and to see that the passenger analogy belongs to the critics. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-077 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Popular accounts of war dwell on generals and battles, but campaigns are more often decided by supply. An army that cannot feed its soldiers, replace its ammunition or move fuel to its vehicles loses the capacity to fight long before it loses a battle. Many celebrated offensives stalled not because the enemy stopped them but because they outran the roads, railways or wagons that sustained them. Brilliant tactics can win an engagement; only a working system of supply can turn a run of engagements into a victory. This is why careful commanders tend to plan the movement of food and fuel before the movement of troops, and why the study of logistics, though unglamorous, explains more about the outcome of wars than the study of battlefield genius.

  1. (A)Careful commanders plan the movement of food and fuel before the movement of troops, and this habit makes them more successful than commanders who plan otherwise.
  2. (B)Popular histories of war ought to be rewritten to drop accounts of generals and battles and to concentrate instead on roads, railways and supplies.
  3. (C)Wars are usually decided less by tactical brilliance in battle than by keeping armies supplied, so logistics explains their outcomes better than generalship does.
  4. (D)Generals who win battles through clever tactics are overrated, since nearly every famous offensive failed once enemy forces managed to cut its lines of supply.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The opening sentence states the thesis that 'campaigns are more often decided by supply', the middle sentences support it, and the last sentence concludes that logistics 'explains more about the outcome of wars than the study of battlefield genius'. The correct answer restates exactly this comparison.

Why not (A): This takes one illustrative detail as the point and adds a comparison of commanders that the paragraph never makes.

Why not (B): The paragraph makes a claim about what explains outcomes; it prescribes no rewriting of popular histories, and it grants that tactics can win engagements.

Why not (D): The paragraph says offensives stalled 'not because the enemy stopped them' but because they outran their own supply, and it speaks of 'Many celebrated offensives', not nearly every one.

Common misconception: Picking the option about commanders' planning because it repeats a detail from the final sentence.

Difficulty: The thesis is stated in the first and last sentences; wrong options are a misread detail, a narrow detail and an added prescription. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-078 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Large premodern empires often invested heavily in relay systems of couriers and stations long before they built much else in common. The reason is less obvious than it seems. A ruler far from his provinces faced a problem not of force but of information: governors might rebel, under-report taxes or simply act on stale orders, and the centre could not correct what it could not see. A fast relay shortened the delay between an event and the capital's knowledge of it, and so shrank the room in which local officials could act unobserved. The roads and horses carried letters, but what they really delivered was the credible prospect of timely oversight. That is why such systems were often reserved for official use rather than opened to merchants and private correspondents.

  1. (A)Courier relays in premodern empires were closed to merchants because private letters would have crowded the roads and delayed the government's own messages.
  2. (B)Premodern empires prized courier relays mainly because quicker news let distant rulers watch provincial officials, narrowing the room for disobedience or deceit to go unnoticed.
  3. (C)Because distant governors routinely rebelled and concealed taxes, premodern rulers came to treat fast relays as their only effective means of keeping control.
  4. (D)Premodern empires built courier relays chiefly to move troops and tax revenue quickly between capital and provinces, which made any rebellion much harder to sustain.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph poses a puzzle (why relays came early), answers it by recasting the ruler's problem as one of information, and explains that speed 'shrank the room in which local officials could act unobserved'. Its last line, 'what they really delivered was the credible prospect of timely oversight', is the point the correct answer captures.

Why not (A): The paragraph explains the restriction by the relays' role in oversight; congestion of the roads is a reason it never gives.

Why not (C): The paragraph says governors 'might' rebel or under-report, not that they routinely did, and it never calls relays the only means of control.

Why not (D): The paragraph says the ruler's problem was 'not of force but of information' and that the relays 'carried letters', so troops and revenue misstate their purpose.

Common misconception: Choosing the troops-and-revenue option because relays sound like military infrastructure.

Difficulty: The correct answer depends on the reframing from force to information; one wrong option uses the force reading and another inflates 'might' into 'routinely'. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-079 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Two accounts of medieval craft guilds have long competed. On one, guilds were cartels: they restricted entry, fixed prices and kept outsiders from the trade, enriching masters at the expense of customers and would-be rivals. On the other, they were institutions of trust: in markets where buyers could not easily judge the quality of cloth or metalwork, a guild's standards and inspections gave its mark a meaning that no single workshop could establish alone. The two accounts are usually presented as rivals, but they describe mechanisms that can coexist in the same institution, and the more useful question is which one predominated under which conditions. Where quality was easy to observe, the trust function had little to add and restriction was likely to dominate; where quality stayed hidden until long after purchase, the same barriers to entry may have been the price of a reputation worth having.

  1. (A)The cartel and trust views of guilds need not be rivals; which function prevailed probably depended on how hard buyers found it to judge quality before buying.
  2. (B)Guilds were primarily institutions of trust rather than cartels, since their limits on entry were simply the price buyers paid for reputations that benefited every customer.
  3. (C)Where the quality of goods could be judged at a glance, guilds served no useful purpose at all, and towns would have done better without them.
  4. (D)The cartel and trust accounts of guilds are both partly right, because every guild restricted entry to some extent and every guild also inspected its members' goods.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph sets out the cartel view and the trust view, then argues that they 'describe mechanisms that can coexist' and that the useful question is 'which one predominated under which conditions'. Its final sentence ties the answer to whether quality was easy to observe or 'stayed hidden until long after purchase'. The correct answer captures both the reconciliation and the condition.

Why not (B): The paragraph refuses to choose one account and says restriction 'was likely to dominate' where quality was easy to observe, so siding wholly with trust contradicts it.

Why not (C): The paragraph says only that the trust function 'had little to add' there; 'no useful purpose at all' and the verdict on towns go beyond it.

Why not (D): The paragraph's point is conditional, that the balance depended on how observable quality was; it makes no universal claim about what every guild did.

Common misconception: Choosing the 'both partly right' option, which sounds balanced but replaces the paragraph's conditional answer with an unsupported universal claim.

Difficulty: Two options sound like reconciliations; only one keeps the condition (observability of quality) that decides between the mechanisms. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-080 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Business writing often treats being first to market as a decisive advantage, and the stories it tells are memorable: the pioneer that defined a category and never let go. Yet such stories are drawn disproportionately from survivors. Pioneers that created a market and were then overtaken by better-funded or more careful followers are forgotten, or are remembered as footnotes to the followers' success, so the sample from which the lesson is drawn is tilted in its favour. Followers also enjoy real benefits: they can learn from the pioneer's mistakes, wait for customers to understand the product and adopt technology that has become cheaper. This does not mean that entering first is never valuable; where customers face high costs of switching, an early lead can harden into dominance. It means that the advantage is conditional, and that the anecdotes usually offered for it cannot establish how often it holds.

  1. (A)Business writers deliberately exaggerate the value of being first to market, picking pioneer stories that suit the lessons they already wish to teach.
  2. (B)Firms that follow a pioneer into a new market generally outperform it, because they learn from its mistakes and adopt technology after it has become cheaper.
  3. (C)Entering a market first pays off only when customers find switching costly, and in every other market it is a handicap that sensible firms ought to avoid.
  4. (D)Entering a market first helps only in some conditions, such as high switching costs; belief in its power rests on stories that forget overtaken pioneers.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph criticises the belief in first-mover advantage on two grounds: the stories behind it come from survivors, and followers have real benefits. It then concedes that early entry can matter 'where customers face high costs of switching' and concludes that 'the advantage is conditional'. The correct answer holds the critique and the concession together.

Why not (A): The paragraph describes a sampling bias toward survivors, not deliberate exaggeration; it attributes no motive to business writers.

Why not (B): The paragraph lists followers' benefits but never says they generally outperform pioneers; it says only that the first-mover advantage is conditional.

Why not (C): Switching costs are offered as one example ('where customers face high costs'), not the sole condition, and the paragraph never calls early entry a handicap to avoid.

Common misconception: Picking the follower option, which turns 'Followers also enjoy real benefits' into a general claim of superiority.

Difficulty: The tempting wrong option reverses the myth instead of qualifying it; the correct answer must keep the concession. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-081 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It might seem that counterfeits can only harm the luxury brands they copy, since each fake sold appears to be a sale lost. But most people who buy an obvious imitation for a small fraction of the price were never going to pay for the original, so the lost sale is often imaginary. The more serious threat is subtler. A luxury good is bought partly for what it signals, and the signal depends on the belief that the item is scarce and costly to obtain. When copies become common enough that observers can no longer tell who paid full price, the original loses part of what its buyers were paying for, even though none of them has been deceived. The harm, in other words, falls not on any transaction between the brand and the buyer of a fake but on the meaning of the logo for everyone else.

  1. (A)Counterfeits harm luxury brands less through lost sales, often illusory, than by blurring which items are genuine and so weakening the status the logo signals.
  2. (B)Luxury brands begin to lose sales to counterfeits once copies become common enough that observers can no longer tell genuine items from imitations.
  3. (C)Counterfeit luxury goods do little real harm to the brands they copy, because the people who buy fakes could never have paid for the genuine articles anyway.
  4. (D)The chief damage done by counterfeits falls on buyers of genuine luxury goods, who are misled into paying full price for items that are no longer scarce.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph first dismisses the obvious harm (lost sales are 'often imaginary'), then identifies 'The more serious threat': a luxury good's signal depends on perceived scarcity, and common copies blur who paid full price. Its last sentence locates the harm in 'the meaning of the logo for everyone else'. The correct answer states both moves.

Why not (B): The paragraph locates the harm 'not on any transaction' but on the logo's meaning; recasting it as lost sales reverses the distinction it draws.

Why not (C): This keeps the first half of the argument and drops the 'more serious threat' to the meaning of the logo, so it contradicts the paragraph's conclusion that harm does occur.

Why not (D): The paragraph says genuine buyers lose part of what they paid for 'even though none of them has been deceived', so 'misled' contradicts it.

Common misconception: Choosing the lost-sales option because it mentions the right condition (copies becoming indistinguishable) while getting the kind of harm wrong.

Difficulty: Every wrong option reuses the paragraph's terms; separating them needs the distinction between harm to sales, harm through deception and harm to a signal. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-082 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Economists tend to defend surge pricing on grounds of efficiency: when demand for rides or rooms spikes, a higher price rations the scarce supply to those who value it most and draws more suppliers in. The reasoning holds within its own terms, but it explains less of the public reaction than its defenders suppose. People who resent a tripled fare during a storm are not usually confused about supply and demand; they are objecting to what the price seems to say, that a seller is profiting from their predicament. Norms of fairness in many communities treat raising prices in an emergency differently from raising them on a busy Saturday, even when the economics are identical. A pricing scheme that ignores this distinction may be efficient on paper and still erode the goodwill on which the seller depends.

  1. (A)Customers accept higher prices on busy weekends but reject them in storms because the increases charged during emergencies tend to be far larger than weekend ones.
  2. (B)Surge pricing may ration supply efficiently, but anger at it stems from fairness norms about profiting from emergencies, which sellers ignore at the cost of goodwill.
  3. (C)Surge pricing is both unfair and inefficient in emergencies, so sellers should hold prices fixed whenever customers are caught in storms or similar predicaments.
  4. (D)Public opposition to surge pricing arises mainly because customers misunderstand how higher prices ration scarce supply and attract extra sellers when demand spikes.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph accepts the efficiency case, then argues that it misses the source of public anger: people object to 'what the price seems to say', and fairness norms treat emergencies differently 'even when the economics are identical'. It ends by warning that such a scheme may 'erode the goodwill on which the seller depends'. The correct answer includes the concession, the explanation and the consequence.

Why not (A): The paragraph says the norms differ 'even when the economics are identical', so explaining the difference by the size of the increase contradicts it.

Why not (C): The paragraph grants that the efficiency reasoning 'holds within its own terms' and offers no rule about fixing prices, so both halves misstate it.

Why not (D): The paragraph says resentful customers 'are not usually confused about supply and demand', so this states the opposite of its explanation.

Common misconception: Choosing the 'unfair and inefficient' option by forgetting that the efficiency argument is conceded.

Difficulty: Requires separating the conceded efficiency point from the fairness explanation; one wrong option contradicts each. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-083 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

In many forests that evolved with frequent low-intensity fire, decades of putting out every blaze have made fires worse rather than rarer. Small fires once cleared away dead wood, needles and young trees at regular intervals, keeping the fuel on the forest floor thin. When those fires were suppressed, the fuel kept accumulating, and dense undergrowth formed a ladder by which flames could climb into the canopy. A fire that would once have crept harmlessly along the ground now meets years of stored fuel and becomes the kind of blaze that kills mature trees and resists control. The policy succeeded at its immediate aim, stopping each fire, while creating the conditions for larger ones. The lesson applies chiefly to fire-adapted forests; in ecosystems where fire was naturally rare, suppression does not have the same effect.

  1. (A)Putting out forest fires is always counterproductive, because fuel builds up in every kind of forest whenever small fires are prevented from burning.
  2. (B)Forest managers should stop fighting fires altogether and let every blaze burn, since small fires once kept forests thin and safe from larger ones.
  3. (C)In forests adapted to frequent small fires, suppressing every blaze lets fuel pile up, so later fires grow larger and more destructive.
  4. (D)Dense undergrowth lets flames climb from the forest floor into the canopy, where they kill mature trees and become very hard to bring under control.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The first sentence states the phenomenon, the middle sentences explain how fuel accumulates when small fires are suppressed, and the last two sentences draw the paradox and limit it to fire-adapted forests. The correct answer states the cause, the effect and the scope.

Why not (A): The last sentence restricts the point to fire-adapted forests and says that where fire was rare 'suppression does not have the same effect', so 'always' and 'every kind' contradict it.

Why not (B): The paragraph explains a consequence of suppression but prescribes no policy, and letting every blaze burn goes well beyond anything it says.

Why not (D): This describes one step in the mechanism and leaves out the cause, suppression of small fires, which is the paragraph's point.

Common misconception: Overlooking the final sentence's limit to fire-adapted forests.

Difficulty: The point and its scope are stated plainly; wrong options are an overgeneralisation, a detail and a prescription. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-084 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A measurement can be precise without being accurate. If a scale consistently reads two kilograms too heavy, repeated weighings of the same object will agree closely with one another, and that agreement may inspire confidence, yet every reading is wrong by the same amount. Precision describes how tightly repeated results cluster; accuracy describes how close they lie to the true value. The distinction matters because the usual way of checking a result, repeating it, reveals only the first. A systematic error survives any number of repetitions untouched, and can be exposed only by comparing the instrument with an independent standard or a different method. Consistency is therefore reassuring about random noise but silent about bias.

  1. (A)A scale that reads two kilograms too heavy gives readings that agree closely with one another, which is why such scales are trusted more than they deserve.
  2. (B)Scientists should stop repeating measurements and rely only on comparisons with independent standards, since repetition cannot reveal any kind of error.
  3. (C)Precise instruments tend to be inaccurate, because the consistency of their readings conceals errors that less precise instruments would reveal through their scatter.
  4. (D)Repeating a measurement shows whether results agree, not whether they are correct; systematic bias can be exposed only by an independent standard or method.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph defines precision and accuracy, then explains that repetition 'reveals only the first', that a systematic error 'survives any number of repetitions' and can be exposed only by 'an independent standard or a different method'. The correct answer captures this distinction and its consequence.

Why not (A): This repeats the illustration without the general point it serves, that repetition cannot reveal systematic error.

Why not (B): The last sentence says consistency is 'reassuring about random noise', so repetition does reveal one kind of error, and the paragraph prescribes nothing.

Why not (C): The paragraph says precision and accuracy are independent ('can be precise without being accurate'), not that precise instruments tend to be inaccurate.

Common misconception: Choosing the option that stretches the paragraph into a rejection of repetition, missing that it still detects random noise.

Difficulty: A single clearly stated distinction; wrong options misread, narrow or overstate it. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-085 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Measurements in many cities have found that streets shaded by mature trees are noticeably cooler on summer afternoons than nearby streets without them, and planting trees has accordingly become a favoured response to urban heat. The finding is robust, but it is easy to draw more from it than it supports. Much of the cooling comes from shade and from water evaporating through leaves, and both depend on the tree being large, healthy and adequately watered; a newly planted sapling in a paved pit provides little of either for years, and in a drought a stressed tree may provide less still. Trees therefore help most where there is space, soil and water for them to mature, and planting programmes judged only by the number of saplings put in the ground may promise relief that arrives late or not at all.

  1. (A)Mature, well-watered trees do cool city streets, but young or stressed trees give little cooling, so counting saplings planted overstates the relief that planting brings.
  2. (B)Streets shaded by mature trees are cooler on summer afternoons mainly because their leaves release water that evaporates and draws heat from the air around them.
  3. (C)Planting trees is an ineffective answer to urban heat, since saplings in paved pits give almost no shade and stressed trees provide no cooling in a drought.
  4. (D)Cities should plant trees only where soil and water are plentiful, and should abandon programmes that put saplings into narrow pits in paved streets.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph states a finding (mature trees cool streets), affirms it, then qualifies what follows from it: cooling depends on size, health and water, so saplings give little for years. Its conclusion is that programmes 'judged only by the number of saplings' may over-promise. The correct answer keeps both the finding and the qualification.

Why not (B): The paragraph credits both 'shade' and 'water evaporating through leaves', and in any case this mechanism is a detail, not the paragraph's point about overreading the finding.

Why not (C): The paragraph calls the cooling finding 'robust' and says trees 'help most' in suitable places, so calling planting ineffective contradicts it.

Why not (D): The paragraph warns against judging programmes by sapling counts but never tells cities to abandon any programme; the rule is an added prescription.

Common misconception: Treating the qualification as a refutation of the finding, or picking the mechanism detail.

Difficulty: A finding-and-qualification paragraph; the strongest wrong option overturns the finding instead of qualifying it. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-086 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is sometimes argued that the scarcity of transitional fossils counts against gradual evolutionary change: if lineages changed slowly, the rocks should be full of intermediate forms. The argument assumes that the fossil record is a fair sample of past life, and it is not. Fossilisation requires rapid burial, suitable sediments and the absence of scavengers, conditions met for a tiny fraction of organisms and far more often for hard-shelled marine animals than for soft-bodied or upland ones. Erosion and the movement of the earth's crust have since destroyed much of what was preserved. Given a record this patchy, gaps are what one would expect under almost any account of change, so their presence cannot by itself decide between gradual and abrupt models. The question has to be settled by those parts of the record that are dense enough to test it.

  1. (A)The fossil record is too incomplete to tell us anything about how evolutionary change happened, so the dispute between gradual and abrupt models cannot be settled.
  2. (B)The scarcity of transitional fossils shows that evolutionary change was abrupt rather than gradual, because slow change would have left many intermediate forms behind.
  3. (C)Since fossils form rarely and unevenly, gaps would appear under nearly any model of change, so only densely preserved sequences can show whether change was gradual.
  4. (D)Gaps in the fossil record arise chiefly because erosion and movements of the crust destroyed most fossils of soft-bodied and upland organisms after they had formed.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph reports an argument from missing intermediates, rejects its assumption that the record is a fair sample, explains why it is sparse and biased, and concludes that gaps 'cannot by itself decide' the question, which must be settled by dense parts of the record. The correct answer captures the reason, the limited conclusion and the way forward.

Why not (A): The last sentence says the question can be settled by 'those parts of the record that are dense enough to test it', so declaring it unsettleable contradicts the paragraph.

Why not (B): This is the argument the paragraph reports and rejects, on the ground that it wrongly assumes the record 'is a fair sample of past life'.

Why not (D): The paragraph says such organisms rarely fossilised in the first place; erosion is a further cause, and in any case the option omits the conclusion about testing models.
