The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Selling more seats than a flight holds looks, at first, like a plain breach of faith, since some passengers who paid will be turned away. Yet the practice rests on a reasonable prediction: on most routes a fairly steady share of ticket holders does not turn up, and a carrier that held every seat for them would fly emptier planes and, in the long run, charge everyone more. The real question is not whether to overbook but how to treat those who are bumped. A system that asks for volunteers and pays them enough to give up their seats turns an occasional surplus of passengers into a voluntary exchange; one that removes people at random, with little compensation, makes them bear a cost that the whole system creates.

  1. (A)Airlines overbook because they can predict no-shows, so passengers who are bumped from a flight have no reasonable ground for complaint about the practice.
  2. (B)Asking volunteers to give up their seats is what allows airlines to keep their fares low on the many routes where some ticket holders do not turn up.
  3. (C)Overbooking is reasonable given predictable no-shows and lower fares, but its fairness depends on paying bumped passengers to volunteer rather than removing them at random.
  4. (D)Because some passengers who have paid are turned away, overbooking is a breach of faith that airlines should give up even if fares rise as a result.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph accepts the case for overbooking (predictable no-shows, lower fares) and moves the question to the treatment of bumped passengers: paid volunteering is fair, random removal is not. The correct answer captures the justification and the condition.

Why not (A): The paragraph says random removal with little compensation makes people 'bear a cost that the whole system creates', which gives them a real ground for complaint.

Why not (B): Lower fares come from overbooking itself, not from asking for volunteers; volunteering bears on fairness to the bumped, so the relation is distorted.

Why not (D): This is the first impression the paragraph reports and then answers with 'Yet the practice rests on a reasonable prediction'.

Common misconception: Taking the defence of overbooking as a defence of any way of carrying it out.

Difficulty: One wrong option accepts the first half and drops the condition; another mixes the two halves into a false causal link. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-261 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Family firms are often contrasted with professionally managed companies as if the first were sentimental and the second rational. In practice each makes a different bet. A family owner who hands control to a child gives up the chance of choosing the best candidate from a wide pool, and the risk is that the firm suffers when an heir is chosen by birth alone. But the family firm also gains something hard to buy: owners who expect their grandchildren to inherit the business may think in decades, protect its reputation and resist the pressure to show quick results. The weakness of family succession and the strength of family ownership spring from the same source, the expectation that the firm will stay in the family.

  1. (A)Family firms are run on sentiment while professionally managed companies decide rationally, which explains why heirs chosen by birth alone so often run those firms badly.
  2. (B)Family firms give up a wide choice of leaders but gain long horizons, both effects stemming from the expectation that the firm will stay in the family.
  3. (C)Family firms outperform professionally managed companies, because owners who expect their own descendants to inherit the business plan in decades rather than in quarters.
  4. (D)Family owners should choose successors from a wide pool of outside candidates, keeping ownership in the family while handing daily management over to hired professionals.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph replaces the sentimental-versus-rational contrast with a trade-off: family succession narrows the choice of leaders, while family ownership encourages long horizons, and both follow from expecting the firm to stay in the family. The correct answer states the trade-off and its single source.

Why not (A): The paragraph rejects the sentimental-versus-rational contrast in its first two sentences, and it speaks only of a 'risk' that heirs harm the firm.

Why not (C): The paragraph presents long-term thinking as one side of a 'different bet', set against the cost of a narrow choice of leaders; it makes no claim that family firms do better overall.

Why not (D): The paragraph prescribes nothing; this combination of family ownership and outside managers is an idea it never raises.

Common misconception: Picking the option that keeps only the strength of family ownership and turns it into overall superiority.

Difficulty: The one-sided 'outperform' option is close to half the argument; the reader must notice the paragraph is a balanced trade-off. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-262 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Textbooks have long used the lighthouse as the model of a good that markets cannot supply: once the light shines, every passing ship benefits, and no owner can make a captain pay for a beam he cannot be stopped from seeing. The example is weaker than it looks. Ships do not merely pass lights; they enter ports, and a charge levied on vessels docking nearby can fund a light without anyone being excluded from its beam. Yet the rescue of the market is also partial. Such a charge works only because some authority, a port or a government that grants the right to collect it, can compel payment at the quay, so the arrangement shows less that private provision succeeds without the state than that the line between private and public provision is drawn in the details of who may collect what.

  1. (A)The lighthouse is a weak example of a good markets cannot fund, since port charges can pay for it, yet such charges need an authority that compels payment.
  2. (B)Because no captain can be stopped from seeing a light, lighthouses can be built and run only by governments and never by private owners at all.
  3. (C)Lighthouses show that private owners can supply such goods with no help from the state, provided that they are allowed to charge ships when they dock.
  4. (D)Port charges are an unfair way to pay for lighthouses, since they make ships that dock pay for a beam that ships merely passing can use for nothing.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph criticises the textbook example (port charges can fund a light) and then limits its own criticism (the charges need an authority to compel payment, so the case blurs rather than settles the private-public line). The correct answer keeps both the critique and its limit.

Why not (B): This is the textbook view that the paragraph calls 'weaker than it looks', pointing to port charges as a way of funding a light.

Why not (C): The paragraph says the arrangement shows 'less that private provision succeeds without the state' than something else, because the charge depends on an authority that compels payment.

Why not (D): The paragraph judges whether port charges work and what they depend on, not whether they are fair; the fairness complaint is outside it.

Common misconception: Treating the critique of the textbook example as a full vindication of private provision.

Difficulty: The tempting wrong option matches the first half of the argument and fails only on the 'rescue of the market is also partial' turn. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-263 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The idea of a keystone species, one whose removal brings an ecosystem's arch tumbling down, has been enormously useful in persuading people that a single unremarkable creature can matter far beyond its numbers. But the image smuggles in assumptions. An arch has one keystone, fixed by its geometry; in living systems the importance of a species often depends on circumstances, so that a predator that holds a community together in one bay may be of little consequence in the next, or may matter only in dry years. Treating keystone status as a permanent property of a species can lead conservation to concentrate on a few celebrated animals while overlooking the conditions that made them important. The metaphor is worth keeping, as long as it is read as describing a role that a species plays in a place, not an identity it carries everywhere.

  1. (A)Because a single unremarkable species can matter far beyond its numbers, conservation should devote its resources to finding the one keystone in each ecosystem.
  2. (B)The keystone metaphor should be abandoned, since no species in a living system ever holds an ecosystem together in the way a keystone supports an arch.
  3. (C)Conservation has wrongly concentrated on predators living in coastal bays, overlooking many less celebrated animals that matter more to their communities in dry years.
  4. (D)The keystone image rightly shows that one species can matter disproportionately, but it should be read as a role that depends on place, not as a fixed trait.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph credits the keystone idea with a real insight, objects that the arch image implies a single, fixed keystone, and concludes that the metaphor is worth keeping if read as 'a role that a species plays in a place'. The correct answer captures the credit, the objection and the conditional conclusion.

Why not (A): The paragraph warns against treating keystone status as permanent and against concentrating on 'a few celebrated animals', so this prescription runs against its point.

Why not (B): The last sentence says 'The metaphor is worth keeping' under a condition, so calling for it to be abandoned contradicts the paragraph.

Why not (C): The bay and the dry years are hypothetical illustrations of how importance varies; the paragraph makes no claim about where conservation has actually concentrated.

Common misconception: Choosing the option that drops the metaphor altogether, which overshoots a critique that ends by keeping it.

Difficulty: The critique sounds strong in the middle sentences, so the reader must weigh it against the concluding 'worth keeping'. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-264 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Tree rings can date a piece of timber to the exact year because of a simple fact about growth: in many climates a tree adds one ring each year, wide in favourable seasons and narrow in harsh ones. Trees of the same species growing in the same region therefore share a pattern of wide and narrow rings, much like a barcode written by the weather. By matching the pattern in an old beam with overlapping sequences from living trees and from progressively older timbers, researchers can build a continuous record reaching back long before any tree alive today, and place the beam within it.

  1. (A)Tree rings record the weather of each year so precisely that they have replaced every other method scientists once used to date ancient objects of any kind.
  2. (B)Old beams can be dated only when they come from trees that were still alive at the time researchers first began to build their records of ring patterns.
  3. (C)Since yearly rings in a region record a shared pattern of good and bad seasons, overlapping sequences can be joined into a long record against which old wood is dated.
  4. (D)The age of a single living tree can be found by counting its rings, since each tree adds exactly one ring in every year of its life in any climate.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph explains a method: annual rings vary with the seasons, trees in a region share the pattern, and overlapping sequences from living and older wood are joined into a continuous record in which an old beam can be placed. The correct answer states the mechanism and the use.

Why not (A): The paragraph explains how ring dating works; it says nothing about other dating methods, let alone that rings have replaced them.

Why not (B): The paragraph says the record reaches 'long before any tree alive today' through progressively older timbers, which contradicts this restriction.

Why not (D): The paragraph says 'in many climates', not any climate, and its point is matching patterns across many trees and timbers, not counting the rings of one tree.

Common misconception: Settling for the familiar idea of counting rings and missing the matching of patterns across trees.

Difficulty: The method is set out step by step in three sentences and each wrong option misstates one of them. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-265 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When mountain glaciers shrink, the rivers they feed do not at first run dry; they often swell. Melting ice releases water that has been stored for centuries, so communities downstream may enjoy unusually generous summer flows just as the glaciers are disappearing. The abundance is borrowed. Once a glacier has shrunk past a certain point, there is less ice left to melt each summer, and flows begin a long decline, eventually falling below the levels people had relied on before the melting began. The danger is that years of plenty encourage new farms and towns to plan around a supply that is about to fall away.

  1. (A)Shrinking glaciers pose no real threat to water supplies, since the ice that melts each summer adds to the flow of the rivers on which communities rely.
  2. (B)Shrinking glaciers swell rivers only for a time before a long decline, and this passing surplus risks luring people into relying on water that will not last.
  3. (C)Communities downstream of glaciers should stop expanding their farms and towns at once, because every river fed by melting ice will soon run completely dry.
  4. (D)River flows fall as soon as mountain glaciers begin to shrink, leaving the farms and towns downstream without the water they had once relied upon.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph reports a counter-intuitive pattern (melting first swells rivers, then flows decline) and draws the risk from it: plenty in the early years encourages planning around water that will fall away. The correct answer keeps the two phases and the danger.

Why not (A): The paragraph calls the extra flow 'borrowed' and describes a later 'long decline', so denying any threat contradicts it.

Why not (C): The paragraph warns about planning around a temporary surplus but prescribes no halt, and the claim that every river will run completely dry goes beyond 'falling below the levels people had relied on'.

Why not (D): The first sentence says rivers 'do not at first run dry; they often swell', so an immediate fall reverses the sequence described.

Common misconception: Assuming that melting glaciers must mean less water from the start.

Difficulty: The reader must keep the order of two phases and the stated danger; one wrong option drops each. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-266 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Planners in dry regions have often judged land by its average rainfall, asking whether a district receives enough water in a typical year to support crops or herds. The question sounds sensible but can mislead badly. In arid places the average is a statistical fiction that few actual years resemble: runs of meagre seasons are broken by an occasional deluge, and the mean sits between them, describing no year that anyone lives through. Herders who move their animals in search of rain and keep flexible claims to distant pasture are responding to this variability, not ignoring good practice, while schemes that settle them on plots sized for an average year can fail in the first drought. Averages are not useless, since over long periods they still say something about a region's water; but where variation is the dominant fact, a plan built on the mean is a plan for a climate that does not exist.

  1. (A)Settlement schemes in dry regions fail mainly because the plots given to herders are too small to support their animals even in a year of average rainfall.
  2. (B)Average rainfall figures are meaningless in dry regions, so planners should rely solely on the knowledge of mobile herders when deciding how such land is to be used.
  3. (C)Because occasional deluges raise the average, dry regions are in most years wetter than their rainfall figures suggest, which is why settled schemes there fail.
  4. (D)Where rainfall in dry regions swings widely, plans built on the average misread real conditions and mobile herding is a sensible response, though averages keep some long-run value.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph argues that in arid places the average describes 'no year that anyone lives through', that herders' mobility answers this variability, and that settlement on average-sized plots fails in drought; it then concedes that averages still say something over long periods. The correct answer keeps the argument, the herding point and the concession.

Why not (A): The paragraph says the plots are 'sized for an average year' and fail 'in the first drought'; the fault is variability, not plots too small for average conditions.

Why not (B): The paragraph says 'Averages are not useless' and recommends no transfer of planning to herders, so this is both extreme and an added prescription.

Why not (C): Deluges pull the mean above the 'meagre seasons' that make up most years, so most years are drier than the average, not wetter; the option reverses the relation.

Common misconception: Accepting the reversed reading of how deluges affect the average, or the extreme option that discards averages entirely.

Difficulty: One wrong option reverses a statistical relation that must be worked out from the text, and another fails only on the final concession. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-267 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When an inferior technical standard becomes universal, it is common to blame the stubbornness of users who will not switch to something better. The explanation misplaces the problem. A standard is valuable largely because others use it: a plug fits more sockets, a file format opens on more machines, a keyboard layout matches the one in the office. A user who switches alone bears the costs of incompatibility while gaining little, so each person's reluctance is reasonable even if everyone would be better off moving together. This does not mean that a dominant standard is always inferior, a claim that is often made and harder to prove; it means only that its dominance is no evidence of its merit.

  1. (A)A widely used standard persists because individuals reasonably refuse to switch alone, so its dominance alone says nothing about whether it is better than the alternatives.
  2. (B)Dominant technical standards are usually inferior to their rivals, because early adoption rather than quality decides which standard becomes universal in the end.
  3. (C)Governments should require users to switch to better standards all together, since no individual will choose to move alone to a superior plug or file format.
  4. (D)Users cling to familiar standards out of stubbornness, which stops better plugs, file formats and keyboard layouts from replacing the worse ones in use.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph replaces the stubbornness explanation with a reason: a standard's value comes from others using it, so switching alone is costly and reluctance is reasonable. It then limits its claim: dominance is no evidence of merit, but that does not show the dominant standard is inferior. The correct answer keeps the cause and the limited conclusion.

Why not (B): The paragraph explicitly declines to claim that a dominant standard is inferior, calling that claim 'harder to prove'.

Why not (C): The paragraph notes that everyone might gain by 'moving together' but prescribes no government action; the remedy is an outside addition.

Why not (D): This is the explanation the paragraph says 'misplaces the problem'; it argues that reluctance is reasonable, not stubborn.

Common misconception: Reading the paragraph as claiming that the dominant standard is worse, which it explicitly refuses to assert.

Difficulty: The 'usually inferior' option sounds like the paragraph's theme and is excluded only by its last sentence. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-268 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Early machine translation was easy to distrust: its sentences were stiff and ungrammatical, and readers could see at once where it had gone wrong. Newer systems produce smooth, natural prose, and this real improvement brings a new and less obvious difficulty. When a translation reads fluently, readers tend to assume it is accurate, yet a fluent sentence can still drop a negation, confuse two names or soften a warning. The very polish that makes the output pleasant to read also hides its mistakes, so errors that once announced themselves now pass unnoticed.

  1. (A)Early machine translation was stiff and ungrammatical, which made readers distrust it and confined its use to rough and informal purposes of little importance.
  2. (B)Newer machine translation systems make more errors than older ones, since producing smooth and natural prose forces them to take liberties with the meaning.
  3. (C)As machine translation has grown fluent, its errors have become harder to spot, since readers mistake smooth prose for accuracy.
  4. (D)Machine translation should not be trusted for any purpose at all, because even its most fluent output routinely drops negations and confuses names.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph contrasts old, visibly faulty translation with new, fluent output and explains the new risk: readers equate fluency with accuracy, so the 'very polish' hides mistakes. The correct answer states the change and its cause.

Why not (A): This covers only the first sentence and adds a claim about limited use that the paragraph never makes; the central point about hidden errors is missing.

Why not (B): The paragraph says errors are harder to notice, not more frequent; it makes no comparison of how many errors the systems make.

Why not (D): The paragraph says a fluent sentence 'can still' make such errors; claiming they happen routinely and ruling out any use overstates it, and it gives no such advice.

Common misconception: Inferring that a new difficulty means more errors rather than less visible ones.

Difficulty: The point is made in the last two sentences and each wrong option fails on one clear word or omission. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-269 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

It is often said that the ease of digital photography has cheapened the photograph: when a picture costs nothing, people take thousands and look at almost none. The complaint has force, but it assumes that a photograph's value lies in being kept and contemplated. Many of today's pictures do a different job. They are taken to be sent, as a way of saying 'here I am' or 'look at this', and their purpose is fulfilled the moment they are seen, much as a spoken remark is not diminished by being forgotten. What has declined is not the photograph's worth but the share of photographs meant to be kept, and the real loss, if there is one, falls on that smaller group, which now lies buried among the rest.

  1. (A)Because digital pictures cost nothing, people take thousands and look at almost none, which shows that photographs have lost much of the value they once had.
  2. (B)Cheap digital photographs have changed in purpose rather than lost value, many now serving as passing messages, though the few meant to be kept may be lost among them.
  3. (C)Photographs taken to be sent are more valuable than those kept in albums, since they fulfil their purpose at once and need never be looked at again by anyone.
  4. (D)People should take far fewer digital photographs, so that the pictures worth keeping are not buried beneath thousands of casual images sent to friends and family.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph grants the complaint some force, rejects its assumption about where a photograph's value lies, reclassifies most pictures as messages whose purpose ends when they are seen, and locates any real loss in the smaller group meant to be kept. The correct answer carries the reclassification and the hedged loss.

Why not (A): This is the complaint the paragraph reports and then answers by saying it wrongly 'assumes that a photograph's value lies in being kept and contemplated'.

Why not (C): The paragraph says sent pictures do 'a different job', not a more valuable one; it ranks neither kind above the other.

Why not (D): The paragraph notes that kept pictures may be buried but recommends nothing; the call to take fewer photographs is an added prescription.

Common misconception: Choosing the reported complaint because the paragraph concedes it 'has force'.

Difficulty: The concession at the start makes the reported view tempting, and the comparative option distorts 'a different job' into 'more valuable'. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-270 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When factories first replaced steam engines with electric motors, the gains in productivity were for a long time disappointing, and some observers concluded that the new power source had been oversold. The disappointment had a simpler cause. Early adopters typically installed one large motor in place of the old engine and kept the rest of the plant unchanged: the same system of shafts and belts, the same buildings arranged around a central drive. Electricity's real advantage, that small motors could be placed wherever work was done, could be exploited only when factories were redesigned around it, and that required new buildings, new layouts and managers who had learned to think in a new way. The lesson is not that every new technology will eventually pay off once organisations catch up, but that its early returns are a poor guide to what it can do when they do.

  1. (A)Any new technology that disappoints at first will deliver large gains once the organisations that use it have had enough time to adapt their methods to it.
  2. (B)Electric motors failed to raise productivity at first mainly because the early models were too large and too weak to take the place of steam engines effectively.
  3. (C)Electric motors raised output slowly because plants had to be redesigned around them, so early results understated their potential, without proving that every new technology pays off.
  4. (D)Electric power was oversold to factory owners, since replacing steam engines with electric motors brought only disappointing gains for a long time after its introduction.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph rejects the 'oversold' conclusion, explains the slow gains by the failure to redesign plants around small, distributed motors, and draws a carefully limited lesson: early returns are a poor guide, but this does not promise that every technology pays off. The correct answer keeps the cause and the limit on the lesson.

Why not (A): The last sentence explicitly says the lesson 'is not that every new technology will eventually pay off once organisations catch up'.

Why not (B): The paragraph blames the unchanged layout of shafts, belts and buildings, not the power of the motors; one large motor was installed by choice, not as a weakness.

Why not (D): This is the conclusion 'some observers' drew; the paragraph rejects it by giving 'a simpler cause' for the disappointment.

Common misconception: Generalising the electric motor case into a promise about all new technologies, which the last sentence rules out.

Difficulty: The over-general wrong option is the natural moral of the story and is excluded only by a negated clause in the final sentence. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-271 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Each generation seems to need its own translations of the great works, and this is sometimes taken as proof that earlier translators failed. Yet a translation ages in a way the original does not. The original belongs to its language at a fixed moment and is read with the allowances we make for the past; a translation is written in the reader's language and is judged as contemporary prose, so its period idioms, once invisible, eventually begin to sound quaint or stiff. A new version therefore need not correct its predecessor. It may simply restore the effect of a text that, in its own time, did not sound old. That is not to say that every retranslation is an improvement; some merely trade one set of mannerisms for another.

  1. (A)Earlier translations of the great works were usually inaccurate, which is why each new generation must replace them with versions that correct their many mistakes.
  2. (B)Original literary works age far more quickly than their translations, because readers judge originals by the standards of contemporary prose in their own language.
  3. (C)Every new translation of a classic improves on the last one, since it restores the freshness that the original text had for its earliest readers in its own time.
  4. (D)Classics are retranslated less because earlier versions failed than because translations, unlike originals, are read as current prose and date, though new versions are not always better.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph rejects the idea that retranslation shows earlier failure, explains instead that translations are judged as contemporary prose and so date while originals are read with historical allowance, and adds that new versions are not always better. The correct answer carries the explanation and the qualification.

Why not (A): This is the inference the paragraph reports ('sometimes taken as proof') and rejects: a new version 'need not correct its predecessor'.

Why not (B): The paragraph says the opposite: originals are 'read with the allowances we make for the past', while translations are judged as contemporary prose.

Why not (C): The last sentence says it is 'not to say that every retranslation is an improvement', since some 'merely trade one set of mannerisms for another'.

Common misconception: Taking the restoring role of a new version as a guarantee of improvement.

Difficulty: The reversal wrong option uses the paragraph's own contrast with the terms swapped, which a quick reader can miss. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-272 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Film studios turn to sequels and series not mainly because audiences lack imagination but because sequels reduce uncertainty. A new film is a costly bet whose outcome is hard to predict; a film built on a known story arrives with characters that audiences already recognise and a record of how many people paid to see the first one. That information is valuable to anyone deciding where to put a large budget. The steady supply of familiar titles therefore says more about the economics of risk than about what viewers would choose if every kind of film were equally easy to finance.

  1. (A)Studios favour sequels chiefly because familiar stories make costly films less risky, so their abundance reflects the economics of uncertainty more than the taste of audiences.
  2. (B)Audiences prefer familiar characters to new ones, which is why studios now make sequels instead of original films that viewers would not pay to go and see.
  3. (C)Sequels are always more profitable than original films, because they arrive with characters that audiences recognise and a record of earlier ticket sales.
  4. (D)Studios ought to finance far more original films, since a steady supply of familiar titles narrows the range of choice that is available to viewers.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph explains a pattern: sequels reduce uncertainty for those placing large budgets, so the supply of familiar titles reflects 'the economics of risk' more than audience choice. The correct answer states the cause and its implication.

Why not (B): The first sentence says studios turn to sequels 'not mainly because audiences lack imagination'; the paragraph places the cause in the studios' risk, not viewers' preferences.

Why not (C): The paragraph says sequels reduce uncertainty, not that they always earn more; the claim that they are always more profitable is extreme and never made.

Why not (D): The paragraph explains why sequels are common but recommends nothing; this prescription is outside it.

Common misconception: Assuming that what is produced must be what audiences most want.

Difficulty: The cause is stated in the first sentence and each wrong option is ruled out by a single phrase. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-273 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The classic detective story asks the reader to accept an unusual bargain: every clue the detective uses must be shown on the page before the solution, so that a sufficiently attentive reader could, in principle, reach it first. The convention turns the novel into a contest between writer and reader, and much of the genre's pleasure comes from losing that contest fairly. But fairness has a price. A writer who must lay out every clue while still surprising the reader is tempted to reduce people to suspects and conversations to evidence, and many such books are remembered for their solutions rather than their characters. The finest examples avoid this by hiding clues inside character itself, so that understanding a person and solving the crime become the same act.

  1. (A)Detective writers should abandon the rule that clues must appear before the solution, so that they are free to develop their characters more fully and freely.
  2. (B)The fair-play convention has ruined detective fiction, since every book written under it is remembered for its solution rather than for its characters.
  3. (C)Showing every clue makes detective fiction a fair contest but tempts writers to flatten characters, a danger the best writers avoid by hiding clues in character.
  4. (D)Detective stories give pleasure mainly because readers usually solve the crime before the detective does, using the clues the writer has laid out on the page.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph describes the fair-play bargain, credits it with the genre's pleasure, names its cost (characters reduced to suspects) and shows how the best writers avoid that cost by hiding clues in character. The correct answer carries the convention, the cost and the way out.

Why not (A): The paragraph shows how the best writers keep the rule while avoiding its cost; abandoning it is a prescription that runs against the paragraph.

Why not (B): The paragraph says 'many such books', not every book, and praises 'The finest examples', so the claim of ruin is extreme.

Why not (D): The paragraph says the pleasure comes from 'losing that contest fairly', and that a reader could solve it only 'in principle'; usually winning reverses this.

Common misconception: Misreading the source of the pleasure as the reader's winning rather than losing fairly.

Difficulty: The first wrong option misreads a single phrase about the contest that many readers skim; the others overstate the cost. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-274 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

'A child could have painted that' is the oldest complaint against abstract art, and defenders usually reply that the painter could also draw a perfect likeness and chose not to. The reply concedes too much. It accepts the critic's assumption that a picture is valuable in proportion to the difficulty of making it, and merely insists that the difficulty lies elsewhere, in the years of training behind the apparent simplicity. But much of what matters in such work is not difficulty at all; it is the decision about what to leave out, the sense of when a canvas is finished, the placing of a single shape so that it holds a whole surface. A child might produce something similar by accident, as a monkey at a keyboard might type a line of verse, without the result being the same kind of achievement. The complaint is answered not by proving the painter skilful but by showing that skill was never the right measure.

  1. (A)Abstract painters deserve respect because most of them could draw a perfect likeness, and their simple canvases conceal years of demanding technical training.
  2. (B)Citing an abstract painter's hidden technical skill accepts the critic's premise that worth tracks difficulty, whereas such work is valued for deliberate choices that a chance likeness cannot equal.
  3. (C)Abstract art cannot really be told apart from the work of children, which shows that its value depends wholly on the reputation of the painter who signs it.
  4. (D)Abstract paintings are harder to make than realistic ones, since deciding what to leave out of a canvas calls for greater skill than drawing a likeness.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph criticises the standard defence of abstract art for accepting that value tracks difficulty, locates value instead in deliberate choices (what to leave out, when to stop, where to place a shape), and concludes that 'skill was never the right measure'. The correct answer captures the critique of the defence and the alternative measure.

Why not (A): This is the defenders' usual reply, which the paragraph says 'concedes too much' by accepting that value depends on difficulty.

Why not (C): The paragraph says a child's accidental likeness is not 'the same kind of achievement', and it never ties value to reputation; the option opposes its argument.

Why not (D): The paragraph says what matters 'is not difficulty at all'; recasting choice as greater difficulty keeps the very measure it rejects.

Common misconception: Choosing the option that relocates difficulty to decision-making, which still treats difficulty as the measure.

Difficulty: Two wrong options defend abstract art in terms of skill or difficulty; separating them from the correct answer needs the paragraph's distinction between difficulty and choice. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-275 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Performing old music on the instruments of its own time has revealed a good deal. Gut strings, valveless horns and lighter keyboards produce textures that modern instruments smooth over, and many listeners have found that familiar works sound clearer and livelier when played this way. Yet the movement's claim to 'authenticity' needs care. We can rebuild the instruments, but not the ears of the original audiences, for whom these sounds were ordinary rather than novel, and much about how the music was actually played is not recorded anywhere. Period performance gives us a valuable new way to hear old music, not the old way restored.

  1. (A)Gut strings, valveless horns and lighter keyboards make familiar works sound clearer and livelier than any modern instruments are able to make those same works sound.
  2. (B)Period performances add nothing of real value, because the original audiences heard these sounds as ordinary and modern listeners can never share their ears.
  3. (C)Old music should be performed only on period instruments, since modern instruments distort the clear and lively textures that the composers of the past originally intended.
  4. (D)Period instruments reveal qualities in old music that modern ones hide, but cannot recreate how it was first heard, so they offer a new hearing, not a restoration.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph credits period instruments with revealing textures modern ones smooth over, then limits the claim to authenticity: the original listeners' ears and many details of playing cannot be recovered. Its conclusion is that period performance is 'a valuable new way to hear old music, not the old way restored'. The correct answer keeps both halves.

Why not (A): This restates a detail from the second sentence and leaves out the central qualification about the limits of 'authenticity'.

Why not (B): The paragraph calls period performance 'a valuable new way to hear old music', which this option directly contradicts.

Why not (C): The paragraph praises period performance but prescribes nothing, and it never claims to know what composers intended.

Common misconception: Picking the detail about clearer textures, which is true but leaves out the qualification.

Difficulty: The point is stated in the last sentence and the wrong options are clearly extreme, opposite or narrow. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-276 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Publishers often keep the translator's name off the cover of a translated novel, on the theory that readers want to feel they are meeting the author directly and that a second name reminds them of an intermediary. The reasoning is understandable, but it rests on a fiction. Every sentence the reader of a translation encounters was chosen by the translator: the rhythm, the register, the jokes that land or fall flat. To hide that person is not to remove the intermediary but to conceal one who is doing a great deal of the work, and the concealment has costs. Readers who do not know a book is translated cannot judge whether an awkward phrase belongs to the author or to the rendering, and translators whose names are buried find it harder to build the reputations that would let them command better fees and better projects. Naming the translator does not spoil the illusion of direct contact so much as make the reader's trust an informed one.

  1. (A)Omitting the translator from the cover conceals, rather than removes, the person who chose every sentence, which hampers readers' judgement and translators' careers; naming them makes trust informed.
  2. (B)A translated novel is really the translator's book rather than the author's, so the translator's name ought to replace, or at least precede, the author's name on the cover.
  3. (C)Publishers hide translators' names because readers dislike translated books, and this preference, though understandable, steadily lowers the quality of the translations that publishers commission.
  4. (D)Because their names are hidden on covers, translators struggle to build reputations and so cannot command the fees and the projects that their considerable work on each novel deserves.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph rejects the publishers' reasoning as resting 'on a fiction': the translator chose every sentence, so hiding the name 'is not to remove the intermediary but to conceal one'. It names two costs (readers cannot tell author from rendering; translators cannot build reputations) and ends by saying naming makes trust 'an informed one'. The correct answer holds the central claim, both costs and the conclusion.

Why not (B): The paragraph says the translator does 'a great deal of the work', not that the book belongs to the translator; it asks only that the translator be named, not ranked above the author.

Why not (C): The publishers' theory is that readers want to feel they meet the author directly, not that they dislike translations, and nothing is said about falling translation quality.

Why not (D): This is one of the two costs listed near the end; it leaves out the central claim that hiding the translator conceals rather than removes an intermediary, and the cost to readers.

Common misconception: Choosing the option about translators' careers because it is concrete and true to the paragraph, without noticing that it is only one of two supporting costs.

Difficulty: The narrow wrong option is accurate and specific, so the correct answer must be preferred on scope rather than truth. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-277 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Abridged editions of classic novels are often defended as a gentle doorway: a twelve-year-old who would abandon an eight-hundred-page original might finish a hundred-page version and come back for the real thing later. The trouble is that what abridgement removes is rarely random. Editors cut digressions, descriptions and the slow passages in which characters think, because these are what make a book long, but they are also what make it the particular book it is. What survives is the plot, and plot is the part of a classic that a film or a summary could deliver just as well. A young reader who finishes such a version may therefore conclude that they have read the book, and that it was merely a story, and see no reason to return. The doorway can easily become a wall.

  1. (A)Defended as a route to the originals, abridged classics tend to keep only plot and cut what makes each book distinctive, so young readers may see no reason to return.
  2. (B)Editors of abridged classics choose their cuts carelessly and at random, which is why the shortened versions of great novels so often fail to hold the interest of young readers.
  3. (C)Children should not be given classic novels until they are old enough to read the complete originals, since the shortened editions are written by editors rather than by the authors themselves.
  4. (D)Abridged editions are valuable because they let young readers finish classic stories they would otherwise abandon, and many of these readers later go on to read the full versions.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph states the defence (abridgements as a 'doorway'), then argues that the cuts remove exactly what makes a book 'the particular book it is', leaving plot, so a reader may think they have read the book and 'see no reason to return'. The correct answer keeps the defence, the mechanism and the consequence.

Why not (B): The paragraph says what abridgement removes 'is rarely random': editors systematically cut digressions and description. It does not claim the versions fail to hold interest.

Why not (C): The paragraph makes no recommendation about when children should read classics, and its objection is to what abridgement removes, not to who wrote the shortened text.

Why not (D): This is the defence the paragraph reports in its first sentence and then rejects; the author argues that the doorway 'can easily become a wall'.

Common misconception: Picking the option that restates the opening defence, which the paragraph sets up only to answer.

Difficulty: The turn ('The trouble is') is explicit and each wrong option is clearly off once it is read. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-278 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Recorded laughter on television comedies is often mocked as a crude instruction to the audience, a machine telling viewers when something is funny. Yet its persistence for decades suggests it answers a real need. Laughter is overwhelmingly a social behaviour: people laugh far more readily in company than alone, and they often laugh less at a joke than at the shared recognition that a joke has been made. A viewer watching a comedy alone at home is deprived of that company, and the track supplies a substitute, a sense of sitting among others who are enjoying the same thing. This explains why the track feels most intrusive to viewers who are themselves watching in a group, since they already have the company it imitates.

  1. (A)Recorded laughter is a crude device that tells audiences when to laugh, and viewers have come to resent being instructed in this way by the people who make television comedies.
  2. (B)People laugh far more readily in company than when alone, and they often laugh more at the shared recognition that a joke has been made than at the joke itself.
  3. (C)Recorded laughter lasts because laughing is largely social: it gives a solitary viewer a stand-in for an audience, which is also why it irritates people already watching together.
  4. (D)Recorded laughter suits viewers who watch comedies in groups, since it adds to the shared enjoyment they already feel, while solitary viewers find the device intrusive and false.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

After reporting the common mockery, the paragraph argues that laugh tracks persist because laughter is social; the track gives a viewer alone 'a sense of sitting among others', and this also explains why groups find it intrusive. The correct answer states the explanation and its corollary.

Why not (A): This is the mockery the paragraph reports and then answers with 'Yet'; the author explains the device as meeting a real need, not as an instruction viewers resent.

Why not (B): This is the premise about laughter, not the point; it says nothing about laugh tracks, the solitary viewer or the group viewer.

Why not (D): This reverses the paragraph, which says the track supplies company to the viewer alone and feels 'most intrusive' to those watching in a group.

Common misconception: Choosing the reversal because both groups are mentioned, without tracking which group the track is said to help.

Difficulty: One wrong option reverses the two groups and another states only the premise, so the reader must track the direction of the explanation. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-279 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Critics of sampling in popular music often argue that a producer who builds a track from fragments of other people's recordings is not composing at all but merely assembling, and that the result borrows its value from the originals. The argument assumes that originality lies in producing sounds no one has produced before. On that test, however, very little music of any period would pass: composers have always worked with inherited scales, forms, rhythms and even melodies, and much admired music is openly built on borrowed tunes. What distinguishes a composer is not the novelty of the materials but what is done with them, the choices of selection, placement and transformation that make a familiar element mean something new. This does not settle whether any particular sampled track is good, or whether the original performers deserve payment; those are separate questions. It shows only that sampling cannot be dismissed as uncreative merely because its raw materials already exist.

  1. (A)Whether a sampled track is creative depends on how good it is and whether the original performers were paid for their work, not on how new its raw materials happen to be.
  2. (B)Sampling is as creative as any other way of composing, so sampled tracks deserve the same respect as wholly original works and their producers owe nothing to the performers they borrow from.
  3. (C)Because composers in every period have borrowed scales, forms and melodies, no music has ever been truly original, and critics should abandon the idea of originality altogether.
  4. (D)The charge that sampling is uncreative locates originality in new materials, a test most music would fail; creativity lies in transforming materials, though this leaves a track's quality and payment unsettled.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph identifies the critics' assumption (originality means new sounds), shows that almost no music meets it, relocates originality in 'selection, placement and transformation', and then limits its own conclusion: quality and payment are 'separate questions'. The correct answer keeps the refutation, the positive account and the limit.

Why not (A): The paragraph calls quality and payment 'separate questions' from creativity; this option turns them into the test of creativity, which distorts the argument.

Why not (B): The paragraph says explicitly that whether performers 'deserve payment' is a separate question it does not settle, and it does not claim every sampled track deserves respect.

Why not (C): The paragraph relocates originality in 'what is done with' materials rather than discarding it; it never says no music is original.

Common misconception: Choosing the option that mentions quality and payment, because those words appear in the paragraph, without noticing that it makes them criteria of creativity rather than separate questions.

Difficulty: Two wrong options reuse the paragraph's qualification and its examples while distorting their role; the correct answer depends on reading the final two sentences as a limit on the claim. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-280 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Style manuals routinely tell writers to avoid the passive voice, and the advice has hardened into a rule that many writers apply without thinking. The case against the passive is real but narrow. A passive sentence can hide the agent ('mistakes were made'), and a long run of passives can make prose feel inert. But the passive also does work that nothing else does as neatly. It lets a writer keep the topic of a paragraph in the subject position, so that a passage about a disease can go on talking about the disease ('it is spread by mosquitoes') rather than lurching to whatever happens to cause it. It lets scientists foreground a procedure rather than the person who carried it out, when the person is irrelevant. The useful question is never whether a sentence is passive but whether the reader needs to know who acted, and what the sentence should be about.

  1. (A)Scientific writing differs from other prose because it describes procedures, so the passive voice, though unsuitable in most writing, is perfectly acceptable in laboratory reports.
  2. (B)The rule against the passive inflates a narrow objection: passives can hide agents or deaden prose but also keep topics in focus, so the reader's needs should decide.
  3. (C)Writers should generally prefer the passive voice to the active, because it keeps the topic of a passage in subject position and directs attention to procedures rather than people.
  4. (D)The passive voice serves mainly to conceal responsibility, as in 'mistakes were made', and style manuals are right to warn writers against using it in serious prose.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph grants the objection ('real but narrow'), lists the passive's uses (keeping the topic in subject position, foregrounding procedure) and ends by replacing the rule with a question about what the reader needs. The correct answer captures concession, counter-case and the replacement test.

Why not (A): Science is one example of the passive's uses; the paragraph also gives the topic-keeping use for any passage and does not call the passive unsuitable elsewhere.

Why not (C): The paragraph defends the passive for particular purposes and accepts the case against it as 'real'; it never says the passive should generally be preferred.

Why not (D): Concealing the agent is the 'real but narrow' case against the passive; the paragraph goes on to describe work the passive does well, so endorsing the rule reverses it.

Common misconception: Choosing the option about science, which is a vivid example, and missing that it narrows a general point.

Difficulty: The correct answer must balance the concession against the defence; two wrong options each keep only one side. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-281 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A news photograph is often treated as the most neutral element of a report: the words may spin, but the camera simply records. Yet every published photograph has been cropped, and cropping is a choice about what the event was. A picture of a single protester shouting at a line of police tells one story; the same frame widened to show a quiet crowd of hundreds behind him tells another, and the wider frame may show that the shouting man was alone. Nothing in either version is false, and no pixel has been altered. The distortion, if there is one, lies entirely in the boundary. That is why a reader who wants to judge a photograph should ask not only what it shows but what its edges leave out.

  1. (A)A photograph of one protester shouting at police can make a peaceful demonstration of hundreds of people look violent and disorderly to those who see it in a newspaper.
  2. (B)News photographs are less trustworthy than written reports, because photographers routinely alter their images to make protests look more dramatic and violent than the events really were.
  3. (C)An unaltered news photograph is still shaped by cropping, since the frame's edges decide what the event seems to be, so readers should ask what lies beyond them.
  4. (D)Newspapers ought to publish every photograph uncropped, so that readers can see the whole scene for themselves and decide on their own what really happened at the event.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph challenges the view that photographs are neutral: cropping 'is a choice about what the event was', the distortion 'lies entirely in the boundary', and readers should ask what the edges leave out. The correct answer states the point, the reason and the advice.

Why not (A): This is the illustration only; it omits the general point that cropping, not falsification, shapes what any news photograph seems to show.

Why not (B): The paragraph stresses that 'no pixel has been altered' and does not rank photographs below written reports; the issue is the frame, not manipulation.

Why not (D): The paragraph prescribes nothing for newspapers; its advice is to readers, to ask what the edges leave out.

Common misconception: Picking the protester example because it is the most memorable sentence.

Difficulty: The thesis and the advice are stated outright; wrong options are an example, an extreme claim and an invented prescription. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-282 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Whether listening to an audiobook counts as reading is usually argued as a question of status, with defenders insisting that the story reaches the mind either way and sceptics treating listening as a lesser substitute. Both sides tend to miss what actually differs. For narrative of moderate difficulty, a competent listener appears to follow and remember the story about as well as a reader does, so the sceptic's claim that listening is shallower is hard to sustain as a general rule. The difference lies in control. A reader sets the pace, slows down at a difficult sentence, glances back to check who said what, and lets the eye run ahead; a listener receives the text at the narrator's speed and must make an effort to go back. For a thriller this hardly matters. For a dense argument, where comprehension depends on rereading, it may matter a great deal. The useful question is therefore not whether listening is reading, but what kind of text is being taken in.

  1. (A)Listening is not generally shallower than reading, but it gives less control over pace and going back, a difference that matters little for stories and possibly much for dense argument.
  2. (B)Audiobooks are an inferior substitute for printed books, since listeners cannot slow down or glance back, and so they understand and remember less of whatever they hear.
  3. (C)Readers and listeners differ mainly in speed, since narrators read faster than most people, so audiobooks suit thrillers better than slow and descriptive literary fiction.
  4. (D)Listening to an audiobook is a form of reading, since the story reaches a listener's mind just as it reaches a reader's, so the debate about its status is pointless.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph rejects both sides of the status debate: listening is not generally shallower (against the sceptics), but there is a real difference, 'control' (against the defenders), which 'hardly matters' for a thriller and 'may matter a great deal' for dense argument. The correct answer keeps both corrections and the dependence on the kind of text.

Why not (B): The paragraph says the claim that listening is shallower 'is hard to sustain as a general rule'; loss of control matters mainly for dense argument, not for whatever is heard.

Why not (C): The difference named is control over pace and rereading, not that narrators are faster, and the contrast drawn is between stories and dense argument, not between kinds of fiction.

Why not (D): This is the defenders' position, which the paragraph says misses 'what actually differs'; the author insists on a real difference in control.

Common misconception: Choosing the defenders' option because the paragraph agrees that listeners follow stories well, and missing that it also insists on a real difference.

Difficulty: The paragraph corrects both camps; each of two wrong options is one camp's view and partly matches the text. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-283 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Teachers and parents have long worried that the abbreviations of text messaging, the dropped vowels and phonetic shortcuts, would corrode children's spelling. Suppose a school compares its pupils and finds that the heaviest users of such abbreviations are, if anything, slightly better spellers than the rest. It would be tempting to conclude that texting improves spelling, but the finding cannot carry that weight. To abbreviate a word playfully a child must usually know how it is spelled in full, so skill with abbreviations may simply be a sign of a comfort with language that the better spellers already had. What the finding does undermine is the fear itself: if abbreviating were steadily eroding spelling, the heaviest abbreviators should be doing worse, not better. A correlation that cannot prove benefit can still be evidence against harm.

  1. (A)The worry about texting and spelling has now been disproved, so schools ought to stop discouraging pupils from using abbreviations in their messages and other informal writing.
  2. (B)That heavy abbreviators spell slightly better cannot show texting helps spelling, since good spellers may simply abbreviate more, but it does tell against the fear that texting harms it.
  3. (C)Correlations between children's habits and their abilities can never tell us anything at all about causes, so a school's comparison of its own pupils is of no value in this debate.
  4. (D)Text messaging improves children's spelling, because abbreviating words playfully requires them to know the full spellings, and the habit keeps reinforcing that knowledge every day.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph uses a hypothetical finding to make a point about evidence: it cannot show texting helps (better spellers may abbreviate more), but it counts against the feared harm, since harm would predict the opposite pattern. The correct answer keeps both halves of this asymmetry.

Why not (A): The paragraph says the finding does 'undermine' the fear and counts as 'evidence against harm', which is weaker than disproof, and it recommends nothing to schools.

Why not (C): The paragraph's last sentence says such a correlation 'can still be evidence against harm', which contradicts the claim that it is of no value.

Why not (D): The paragraph calls this conclusion 'tempting' and says the finding 'cannot carry that weight'; knowing full spellings is offered as a reason good spellers abbreviate, not as a benefit of texting.

Common misconception: Choosing the 'disproved' option because the paragraph does undermine the fear, and missing the gap between evidence against a claim and disproof of it.

Difficulty: The point is an asymmetry about evidence; wrong options take one half too far. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-284 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Textbook writers often add vivid asides to dry material: an anecdote about a scientist's eccentricities in a chapter on electricity, a dramatic photograph of lightning beside a diagram of charge. The intention is to hold interest, and readers do report finding such pages more enjoyable. Yet experiments on learning from text have repeatedly suggested that interesting but irrelevant details can reduce how much of the central explanation students remember and can apply, apparently by drawing attention and memory towards themselves. This does not mean that interest is the enemy of learning. Details that are vivid and also carry the core idea, such as an example that shows the principle at work, do not seem to carry the same cost. The lesson is that engagement should be built from the material that is to be learned, not borrowed from material beside it.

  1. (A)Irrelevant details in textbooks harm learning chiefly because they make pages longer, so that students spend less of their limited reading time on the central explanation.
  2. (B)Students enjoy textbook pages with vivid anecdotes and dramatic photographs more than plain pages, and this enjoyment makes them more willing to study the central explanation.
  3. (C)Textbooks should be written in plain language without anecdotes, photographs or examples, since anything that makes a page more enjoyable will distract students from what they are meant to learn.
  4. (D)Engaging but irrelevant textbook asides can divert attention from the explanation and weaken learning, though vivid material embodying the idea seems not to; interest should come from content.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph reports a finding (irrelevant but interesting details can reduce learning of the main explanation), qualifies it (relevant vivid details do not carry the same cost), and draws the lesson that engagement should come from the material itself. The correct answer holds finding, qualification and lesson.

Why not (A): The mechanism suggested is that such details draw 'attention and memory towards themselves', not that they lengthen the page or use up reading time.

Why not (B): The paragraph grants the enjoyment but says irrelevant details can reduce what students remember of the explanation; the claim of greater willingness to study is not in it.

Why not (C): The paragraph says interest is not 'the enemy of learning' and approves vivid examples that show the principle at work, so banning them contradicts it.

Common misconception: Choosing the extreme option because the finding is against decorative detail, and ignoring the qualification about vivid examples.

Difficulty: The correct answer depends on keeping the qualification; one wrong option is an overstated version of the finding. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-285 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Open-book examinations are sometimes dismissed as easy, on the assumption that a student who may consult notes need not have learned anything. Anyone who has sat one knows otherwise. Because the facts are available, the examiner cannot reward their mere recall and must instead ask questions that require using them: applying a principle to an unfamiliar case, weighing two sources, building an argument under time pressure. A student who has not understood the material gains little from the book on the desk, since there is no time to learn a subject in the middle of the paper; such students tend to spend the hour leafing anxiously through pages. Open-book examinations do not lower the bar; they move it from remembering to thinking.

  1. (A)Open-book examinations are not easier but differently demanding: since facts can be looked up, they test the application of understanding, which notes cannot supply in the time available.
  2. (B)Students who have not understood a subject spend open-book examinations leafing anxiously through their notes, and so they often fail to finish the paper.
  3. (C)Open-book examinations are easy because students may consult their notes, so they reward the students who take careful notes rather than those who truly understand the subject.
  4. (D)Closed-book examinations ought to be abolished, since testing the recall of facts that anyone can look up wastes students' time and teaches them nothing useful.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (A)

The paragraph rebuts the view that open-book examinations are easy: available facts force questions that require using them, and notes cannot substitute for understanding under time pressure. Its last sentence states the point: the bar moves 'from remembering to thinking'.

Why not (B): This is one supporting detail, and the claim that such students fail to finish is added; the option misses the main point that the bar moves from remembering to thinking.

Why not (C): This is the dismissal the paragraph rejects in its second sentence; the author argues that notes help little without understanding.

Why not (D): The paragraph defends open-book examinations but says nothing against closed-book ones and recommends no abolition.

Common misconception: Choosing the detail about students leafing through pages because it is concrete.

Difficulty: The conclusion is stated in the last sentence and each wrong option is plainly off. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-286 · Para summary · DifficultMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Debates over whether schools should still teach joined-up handwriting are usually framed as a contest between tradition and efficiency: cursive is a heritage skill, keyboards are what adults actually use. The framing obscures the fact that the two sides are often talking about different things. The case for teaching some handwriting is fairly strong, since forming letters by hand appears to help young children learn to recognise them, and much early schoolwork is still done with a pencil. But that case is about handwriting in general, not about the particular joined style, and an argument for one is easily mistaken for an argument for the other. The case for cursive specifically rests on weaker grounds: claims that it is faster, or that it builds discipline, are rarely as well supported as their advocates assume. A school could therefore drop cursive and keep handwriting without any inconsistency.

  1. (A)Cursive should continue to be taught because forming letters by hand helps young children learn to recognise them, which is a benefit that typing on a keyboard cannot provide.
  2. (B)Schools should stop teaching handwriting altogether, because keyboards are what adults actually use and the supposed benefits of cursive are rarely supported by evidence.
  3. (C)The cursive debate merges two questions: the fairly strong case for teaching handwriting does not carry over to the joined style, whose particular benefits are less well supported.
  4. (D)The debate over cursive is at bottom a contest between tradition and efficiency, and efficiency should prevail because most adult writing is now done on keyboards.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (C)

The paragraph's central move is a distinction: the case for handwriting in general is 'fairly strong', but 'an argument for one is easily mistaken for an argument for the other', and the case for cursive specifically 'rests on weaker grounds'. The conclusion follows that a school can drop cursive and keep handwriting. The correct answer states the distinction and the asymmetry of support.

Why not (A): This makes exactly the error the paragraph identifies: it uses the case for handwriting in general as an argument for the particular joined style.

Why not (B): The paragraph calls the case for handwriting 'fairly strong' and says a school could keep handwriting while dropping cursive; abandoning handwriting contradicts it.

Why not (D): The paragraph says this framing 'obscures' what is at issue, so presenting the debate in these terms and picking a side misses its point.

Common misconception: Choosing the pro-cursive option because the letter-recognition point is presented as well supported, and missing that it supports handwriting, not cursive.

Difficulty: The tempting wrong option uses the paragraph's strongest evidence in exactly the way the paragraph warns against; separating them needs the general versus specific distinction. · Exams: CAT, XAT

CAT-VARC-C10-287 · Para summary · MediumMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

University league tables are defended as a service to applicants, who would otherwise have to choose among institutions they know little about. The defence has some force, but it overlooks what a single ranked list does. Each table combines many measures, such as research output, staff numbers per student and graduate salaries, into one score, and the weights given to each are a choice made by the compiler, not a fact about universities. Different weights would produce a different order. An applicant who wants small classes and an applicant who wants a strong research culture are served by different universities, yet both are handed the same list as if it settled which is best. A table that published its components and let readers set the weights would serve applicants better than one that pretends a single verdict exists.

  1. (A)Applicants who want small classes should ignore league tables, since the tables systematically favour universities with strong research over those that give students personal attention.
  2. (B)League tables are worthless to applicants, because the measures they combine, such as research output and graduate salaries, have nothing to do with the quality of a university's teaching.
  3. (C)Compilers of league tables deliberately choose their weights so that famous universities stay at the top, which misleads applicants about where they ought to apply.
  4. (D)League tables inform applicants, but by merging many measures into one score with weights the compiler chose, they imply one best order where other priorities would rank differently.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (D)

The paragraph concedes the tables help applicants, then argues that combining measures with chosen weights produces an order that is not 'a fact about universities', so different applicants are wrongly given one verdict. It proposes publishing components so readers can set weights. The correct answer keeps the concession and the central objection.

Why not (A): The paragraph claims no bias toward research; its point is that any fixed weighting serves some applicants' priorities and not others'.

Why not (B): The paragraph grants the defence 'some force' and objects to the single weighted score, not to the measures; it never says they are unrelated to teaching.

Why not (C): The paragraph says the weights are 'a choice made by the compiler', not that they are chosen dishonestly; motives are never discussed.

Common misconception: Choosing the option about deliberate manipulation, reading 'a choice made by the compiler' as an accusation.

Difficulty: Wrong options add motives or biases that the paragraph does not assert, and each looks like a natural extension of it. · Exams: CAT, XAT, NMAT, SNAP, CMAT, MAH-CET

CAT-VARC-C10-288 · Para summary · EasyMCQ
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

For a long time, people who hurt their backs were told to lie down and stay down until the pain passed. Current guidance for ordinary, short-lived low back pain has largely reversed this advice: staying as active as the pain allows tends to bring a quicker recovery than prolonged rest, which can stiffen muscles and make a return to normal life harder. This does not mean that a patient should ignore pain or push through heavy work, and a day or two of reduced activity in the worst phase may be sensible. Nor does the advice apply to back pain caused by serious injury or disease, which needs proper assessment. The change is narrower than a slogan like 'keep moving' suggests, but within its range it is clear.

  1. (A)People with back pain should keep moving and work through the pain, since rest of any kind stiffens the muscles and delays the patient's return to normal daily activity.
  2. (B)For ordinary short-term back pain, staying reasonably active usually aids recovery better than long bed rest, though brief rest may help and serious causes need separate assessment.
  3. (C)Back pain that is caused by serious injury or disease needs careful assessment by a doctor before a patient decides whether to rest or to stay active.
  4. (D)Doctors were wrong for many years to recommend bed rest for back pain, which shows that medical advice about common complaints should not be trusted by patients.
Answer and explanation

Answer: (B)

The paragraph reports a finding (activity aids recovery from ordinary back pain better than prolonged rest) and then limits it twice: brief rest may be sensible, and serious causes are excluded.
